## The pipeline rewrites the column first {#sec-feature-pipeline}

![A machine-learning pipeline from data collection through feature transformation, selection, dimension reduction, and modelling, with model evaluation and tuning circled.](figures/sources/egu-feature-pipeline.png){fig-alt="Flow chart. Data collection and a feature database feed preparation, then feature extraction and transformation, feature selection, and dimension reduction, then modelling. Model evaluation and tuning is circled and feeds back." width="78%"}

[Hartmann and Rudolph](https://github.com/soga-lab/EGU2026_SC), EGU 2026 short course SC2.28, draw the usual order. The circled step is where the score is judged. A rewrite of the column that changes the mean shows up there as a number you cannot interpret. This hour is about that rewrite.

::: {.notes}
Trace the pipeline left to right and linger on the circled evaluation box. Ask what happens if a log or library-size normalisation is applied before the model is chosen—the metric still looks fine while the estimand changed. This slide sets the stake for everything that follows about transforms versus links.
:::
## A Gaussian is not the default {.center .pitfall-divider background-gradient="linear-gradient(160deg, #f7f4ef 0%, #d6e2f5 100%)"}

## The shape is often the scientific object {#sec-shape}

Environmental $Y$ is often:

- skewed, and strictly positive
- a count, or a composition
- full of zeros, or censored at a detection limit
- dependent in time or in space

A Gaussian `lm` can still be a useful approximation for a mean. It is a poor default when the [support]{.mark} of $Y$ makes the approximation impossible. This hour follows [where we go deeper](#sec-deeper). Skew, in particular, is ordinary: [Quetilismus](#sec-quetilismus).

::: {.notes}
Read the bullet list as a checklist against CA-SYS and SPRUCE: counts, zeros, composition, dependence. The closing sentence is deliberately soft—a Gaussian mean can be fine—before the support argument bites. Link forward to Quetilismus as the cultural habit behind ignoring skew.
:::
## Quetilismus {#sec-quetilismus}

🔗 [Adrian Olszewski](https://www.2kmm.pl/blog/On-the-ubiquity-of-skewness-in-nature/) names the habit after Edgeworth's word for Quetelet. A unimodal curve is treated as a normal curve. Skew is then a [defect]{.mark} to repair: drop the tails, wait for a larger sample, or transform until the histogram looks symmetric.

::: {.notes}
Name Quetilismus once, then list the three repairs: trim tails, wait for $n$, transform until symmetric. Students often recognise their own lab practice in the third.
:::
## A product is not a sum

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
The classical central limit theorem is a statement about a **sum**, and it needs a finite variance. A product of positive steps is a different limit. Cascades, growth, and decay land on a [log-normal]{.mark}, which is skewed. Cauchy, Lévy, and Pareto sit outside that classical sum.
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
![](figures/generated/sketch-nongauss-a-sum-product.png){.sketch fig-alt="Hand-drawn comparison: a sum of steps gives a symmetric blue bell, a product of steps gives a red curve skewed to the right."}
:::
::::

Species abundance and environmental concentrations are on the product side ([Limpert, Stahel, and Abbt, 2001](https://doi.org/10.1641/0006-3568(2001)051[0341:LNDATS]2.0.CO;2); [Andersson, 2021](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-96010-6)). More rows do not turn a product into a sum.

::: {.notes}
Contrast sum versus product in one sentence each; Cauchy and Pareto are the "finite variance fails" examples. The carbon examples at the bottom are the punchline—bigger $n$ does not Gaussianise a multiplicative process. Ask whether read counts feel more like sums or products.

**Going further.** The Lindeberg–Lévy theorem says that $\sqrt{n}(\bar{Y} - \mu)/\sigma$ converges to $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ for independent, identically distributed terms with finite variance $\sigma^2$. Taking logs turns a product $\prod_k U_k$ of positive, independent factors into a sum $\sum_k \log U_k$, so the same theorem gives a log-normal limit whenever $\operatorname{Var}(\log U_k)$ is finite. Without a finite variance the generalised central limit theorem replaces the Gaussian by a stable law (Cauchy and Lévy are members), with a slower, non-$\sqrt{n}$ scaling. Gnedenko and Kolmogorov, *Limit Distributions for Sums of Independent Random Variables* (1954), is the classical source; Limpert, Stahel, and Abbt (2001) give the applied log-normal case.
:::
## Skew is a description {#sec-skew-summary}

A skewed description of a real process does not become less legitimate because the sample grew. Treating the normal law as the dominant description sets aside the mechanisms that generate the skew.

The next slide is the modelling consequence. The Gaussian assumption, when it is used, is about $Y \mid \mathbf{x}$, not about the [raw histogram]{.mark}.

::: {.notes}
Quote the Medium opening idea: skew is not illegitimate because $n$ grew. Bridge to the next slide with the conditional phrase $Y \mid \mathbf{x}$. A common misread is to treat marginal skew as proof the linear model failed before any covariates are in the model.
:::
## Read the conditional shape {.center .pitfall-divider background-gradient="linear-gradient(160deg, #f7f4ef 0%, #d4efe8 100%)"}

## The assumption is conditional

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
A QQ plot of the raw column $Y$ answers the wrong question.

The Gaussian linear model assumes that the **conditional** distribution $Y \mid \mathbf{x}$ is Gaussian, with constant variance. In residual form,

$$
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2).
$$

Look at [residuals]{.mark}, or at a residual QQ plot. Do not gate the analysis on a test of the marginal histogram.
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
![](figures/generated/sketch-nongauss-a-conditional.png){.sketch fig-alt="A blue regression line with three green bell curves drawn sideways along it, one at each of three x values, labelled Y given x."}
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Walk the displayed $Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i$ and stress $\varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)$ as conditional on $\mathbf{x}$. The bold phrase "conditional distribution" is what students should underline. Raw-column QQ plots are the wrong object—say that twice.

**Going further.** The residual $e_i = Y_i - \hat{\mu}_i$ is not the error $\varepsilon_i$: $\operatorname{Var}(e_i) = \sigma^2(1 - h_{ii})$, and the residuals are correlated because $\mathbf{e} = (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{H})\mathbf{Y}$. Standardised residuals $e_i / \{\hat{\sigma}\sqrt{1 - h_{ii}}\}$ correct the unequal variance and are what `plot.lm` uses. For a GLM with a discrete $Y$ the Pearson and deviance residuals are not Gaussian even when the model is right; randomised quantile residuals (Dunn and Smyth, *Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics*, 1996) are exactly standard normal under a correct continuous model and approximately so for discrete ones. The `DHARMa` package uses the simulated version of the same idea.
:::
## How to read the plot :mag:

Points along the line support the reference shape. A curve, or a tail that leaves the line, is a [departure]{.mark}. Illustrative residuals, seed 20261005.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
qq_gaussian <- bind_rows(
  tibble(model = "Gaussian lm, Gaussian Y", residual = resid(fit_lm_gauss)),
  tibble(model = "Gaussian lm, Poisson Y", residual = resid(fit_lm_count))
)
ggplot(qq_gaussian, aes(sample = residual)) +
  stat_qq_line() +
  stat_qq() +
  facet_wrap(~model)
```

::: {.notes}
This slide is code only; the figure is next. Point at `facet_wrap(~model)` and the two residual columns—Gaussian $Y$ versus Poisson $Y$ through the same `lm`. Ask which panel they expect to bend before you advance. Seed 20261005 is illustrative, not field data.
:::
## How to read the plot :mag: {#sec-qq-read}

![Two QQ plots. Left: residuals from a Gaussian response sit near the reference line. Right: residuals from a Gaussian linear model fitted to Poisson counts bend up in the right tail.](figures/generated/qq-gaussian-vs-count.png){fig-alt="QQ plots comparing Gaussian linear-model residuals when the response is Gaussian and when the response is a Poisson count." width="96%"}

::: {.notes}
Pair with the previous code slide: left panel is the sanity check, right panel is the misspecified count. Finger the right-tail lift as variance growing with the mean, not "non-normality" in the abstract. The preceding slide showed how those panels were produced.
:::
## The ends are allowed to wander

[Rodrigue](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/normality-tests-q-q-plots-natalie-rodrigue-qxlqc/): the horizontal axis is the quantile under the reference distribution. The vertical axis is the observed quantile. A straight line, with extra scatter at the ends, is the reference. [Order statistics]{.mark} are noisier in the tails. A systematic curve is the departure. The named shapes are the [shape figures](#sec-qq-shapes).

![](figures/generated/sketch-nongauss-a-qq-wander.png){.sketch fig-alt="Two hand-drawn QQ plots. Left, green points follow the grey line with the two end points a little off it, marked fine. Right, red points curve away from the line in a systematic bend, marked wrong." fig-align="center"}

::: {.notes}
Axes first: theoretical quantile horizontal, sample quantile vertical. Distinguish tail scatter (allowed) from a systematic bend (signal). Link to the four-shape figure before students memorise test names. Thirty seconds unless someone asks about order statistics.

**Going further.** For the sample $p$-quantile, $\operatorname{Var}\{\hat{F}^{-1}(p)\} \approx p(1 - p) / [n\, f\{F^{-1}(p)\}^2]$, where $f$ is the density. In the tails $f$ is small, so the variance of the extreme order statistics is large even under the reference model: that is why the ends wander. For uniform order statistics the exact law is $U_{(i)} \sim \mathrm{Beta}(i, n + 1 - i)$, which is the basis of exact pointwise and simultaneous QQ bands. David and Nagaraja, *Order Statistics* (2003), give the asymptotics.
:::
## A normality test is a poor gate

- with a large $n$, the test rejects a departure too small to change $\hat{\mu}$
- with a small $n$, it misses a departure large enough to matter
- the $p$-value does not say whether the **estimand** is distorted
- the test is aimed at the wrong object if you apply it to raw $Y$ rather than to the model you will trust

Prefer the QQ plot, and then a [likelihood]{.mark} that matches $Y$. A formal test is a poor substitute for that plot.

::: {.notes}
Step through the four bullets; the third is the estimand point students miss. Large $n$ makes the fourth bullet bite—testing raw $Y$ when the model is conditional. Close with the QQ-plus-likelihood recipe on the slide.

**Going further.** A consistent goodness-of-fit test has power tending to 1 against any fixed alternative, so with enough data it rejects departures that change nothing about $\hat{\mu}$. Meanwhile the $t$ statistic is asymptotically valid without Gaussian errors, with an error in the null distribution of order $n^{-1/2}$ controlled by the skewness (the Berry–Esseen bound). Choosing the second test on the result of a first one is a conditional procedure whose overall type I error is no longer the nominal level; Rochon, Gondan, and Kieser (*BMC Medical Research Methodology*, 2012) simulate this for the two-sample case and recommend against the pretest.
:::
## Two sample sizes, two failures

Adrian Olszewski's rule, which this hour follows: stop using them, except when a reviewer demands the number. He counts more than 90 procedures.

- A small sample leaves them [underpowered]{.mark}, so a real departure often passes.
- Past about 150–200 observations they reject almost any departure, including one too small to matter, while the central limit theorem for a **mean** is improving.
- Families aimed at skew, at kurtosis, and at the whole distribution contradict one another. Shapiro–Wilk is one of those families, not a universal test.

::: {.notes}
Give Olszewski's "stop using them" line, then the 150–200 observation remark and the small-sample underpowering bullet. "More than 90 procedures" is rhetorical scale—do not treat it as a number to defend. Shapiro–Wilk is one family among many contradictory ones.
:::
## The same sample, opposite answers

![A normal QQ plot with a step, two histograms of the same sample, and a table of normality-test p-values that disagree.](figures/sources/qq-versus-normality-tests.png){fig-alt="For a sample of 400 with skewness near zero and kurtosis near 3, the QQ plot steps in the middle and the histogram has two modes. Shapiro–Wilk gives 0.123. Several moment tests do not flag the sample. Lilliefors, Cramér–von Mises, and Anderson–Darling do." width="92%"}

$n = 400$, skewness about 0, kurtosis about 3. Shapiro–Wilk gives $p = 0.123$. Lilliefors, Cramér–von Mises, and Anderson–Darling reject. The QQ plot shows the step either way.

::: {.notes}
Restate $n=400$ and the step in the QQ plot before reading any $p$-values. Shapiro–Wilk 0.123 versus rejecting Lilliefors/AD is the lesson—tests disagree while the plot stays honest. Ask which diagnostic they would trust for choosing a family.
:::
## Four shapes on the QQ plot {#sec-qq-shapes}

![Four normal QQ plots: Gaussian points on the line, heavy tails as an S-curve, right skew as a concave-up bend, light tails as a flat S.](figures/sources/qq-four-shapes.png){fig-alt="Four QQ plots against a normal reference. Gaussian points follow the line. Heavy tails flare at both ends. Right skew bends concave-up. Light tails make a flatter S." width="96%"}

Ends that flare are [heavy tails]{.mark}. A concave-up bend is [right skew]{.mark}. A concave-down bend is left skew. A flat S is light tails. The shaded ribbon on the Gaussian panel is a generic band. The band to use is the [tail-sensitive one](#sec-qq-band).

::: {.notes}
Point at each panel in the four-shape figure while naming flare, concave-up, concave-down, flat S. The generic ribbon on the Gaussian panel is not the tail-sensitive band—preview the `bandType = "ts"` slide. Students confuse heavy tails with right skew; keep the vocabulary separate.
:::
## Jumps, steps, and stray points

[Rodrigue](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/normality-tests-q-q-plots-natalie-rodrigue-qxlqc/) names three patterns that are not a smooth curve.

::: {.incremental}
- A jump or a gap: two groups pooled, or a rounding artefact.

- A [staircase]{.mark}: a discrete or heavily rounded response. The residuals keep that discreteness.

- One or two points off an otherwise straight line: outliers. Check whether they move the fit before deleting them.
:::


Below about 30 observations, even a Gaussian sample wiggles. Do not read that noise as a new shape.

::: {.notes}
Step the three fragments: pooled groups, discrete $Y$, outliers. The $n<30$ rule is on the slide—use it to stop over-interpretation. Ask which pattern they have seen in sequencing residuals (often staircase or stray points).
:::
## The straight line is the Gaussian case

![A grid of QQ plots and histograms for Gaussian, beta, uniform, skewed, bimodal, truncated, discrete, and outlier samples.](figures/sources/qq-distribution-gallery.png){fig-alt="Sixteen distributions. Each row shows a normal QQ plot and the matching histogram. Only the Gaussian row follows the reference line. Skew bends the plot, bimodality steps it, and heavy tails flare the ends." width="96%"}

Click the figure. Each distribution is a QQ plot against a normal reference, then the histogram. Only the Gaussian row stays on the line. The others are the shapes from the previous slide, including discrete samples and a sample with outliers.

::: {.notes}
Lightbox the gallery if time allows; otherwise name beta, uniform, bimodal, discrete rows. Only the Gaussian row tracks the line—everything else reuses the vocabulary from the four-shape slide. About one minute with the clickable figure.
:::
## A tail-sensitive band {#sec-qq-band}

The ribbon to draw is the simultaneous [tail-sensitive band]{.mark} of [Aldor-Noiman and colleagues (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.2013.847865). In [`qqplotr`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=qqplotr) that is `bandType = "ts"`. It is implemented for a **normal** QQ plot. A pointwise ribbon is a different object.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
ggplot(residuals, aes(sample = residual)) +
  qqplotr::stat_qq_band(bandType = "ts") +
  qqplotr::stat_qq_line() +
  qqplotr::stat_qq_point()
```

Points outside that band are the departure. A $p$-value from a normality test is not a summary of the same picture. The workshop residuals are the [two QQ plots](#sec-qq-read) above, read this way.

::: {.notes}
Highlight `bandType = "ts"` in the code chunk—normal QQ only. Contrast simultaneous tail-sensitive band with a pointwise ribbon. Tie back to the generated Gaussian-versus-count residuals once students see points outside the band.

**Going further.** A pointwise 95% band covers each quantile with probability 0.95, so with $n$ points the chance that at least one falls outside is far above 5%. A simultaneous band is calibrated so that the whole curve lies inside with probability 0.95. Aldor-Noiman and colleagues (*The American Statistician*, 2013) build it from the $\mathrm{Beta}(i, n + 1 - i)$ law of uniform order statistics, which keeps the band narrow in the tails where a Kolmogorov–Smirnov band is too wide. The calibration assumes the reference family is right up to location and scale, which are estimated.
:::


## Three means, three questions {#sec-three-means}

![Table of the arithmetic, geometric, and harmonic means, with formulas and the inequality A at least G at least H.](figures/sources/arithmetic-geometric-harmonic.jpeg){fig-alt="Three columns. Arithmetic mean is a sum divided by n. Geometric mean is the n-th root of a product. Harmonic mean is the reciprocal of the mean of reciprocals. For positive numbers, A is at least G, which is at least H." width="78%"}

[Sharmi Murali](https://medium.com/@sharmi.v.murali/arithmetic-mean-vs-geometric-mean-vs-harmonic-mean-b956cf1b2b3f): a sum, a product, or a reciprocal. $A \ge G \ge H$ for positive numbers, with equality only when every value is the same. A product process wants $G$, and logging $Y$ [changes the estimand](#sec-log-estimand) to that mean.

::: {.notes}
Walk the three columns in the figure: sum, product, reciprocal. $A \ge G \ge H$ is the inequality to remember. Link logging $Y$ to the geometric mean and forward to the log-estimand slide—students often report $A$ after a log transform.

**Going further.** $A \ge G$ is Jensen's inequality for the concave $\log$: $\overline{\log x} \le \log \bar{x}$. For a log-normal $Y$ with $\log Y \sim \mathcal{N}(m, s^2)$, the geometric mean is $e^{m}$ (the median) and the arithmetic mean is $e^{m + s^2/2}$, so the gap grows with the log-scale spread. $G \ge H$ follows by applying $A \ge G$ to the reciprocals.
:::
## A box plot hides the shape

A box plot reports a median, a box, and whiskers. It does not show a second mode, a pile of ties, or how many points sit in the tail. [The case against using it alone](https://medium.com/data-science/why-a-box-plot-should-not-be-used-alone-and-some-plots-to-use-it-with-23381f7e3cb6) is that those are often the features a carbon response actually has.

Prefer a plot that keeps the raw points. A [raincloud]{.mark} adds a density and a short summary beside them ([Scherer, 6 June 2021](https://www.cedricscherer.com/2021/06/06/visualizing-distributions-with-raincloud-plots-and-how-to-create-them-with-ggplot2/)).

::: {.notes}
List what a box plot hides: bimodality, ties, tail mass. Carbon responses often have those features. Raincloud is the constructive alternative named on the slide—density plus points plus a small summary.
:::
## Show the difference, not a star {#sec-gardner-altman}

![Five panels from Ho and colleagues: a bar chart, a box plot, a scatter with means, a null distribution of the difference, and a Gardner–Altman plot of the mean difference with an interval.](figures/sources/gardner-altman-figure-1.png){fig-alt="Figure 1 of Ho and colleagues. Panels a to c summarise two groups. Panel d shows a permutation null for the mean difference and a p-value. Panel e shows the mean difference, its bootstrap distribution, and a 95 percent interval on a difference axis." width="86%"}

[Ho and colleagues](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-019-0470-3). Panel e is the graphic this workshop keeps: $\Delta$ and an interval.

::: {.notes}
Scan panels a–c as what not to stop at, then land on panel e: mean difference $\Delta$ with an interval on a difference axis. Contrast with a lone star or $p$-value. This is the reporting standard the pitfalls section keeps returning to.
:::
## Keep the question, change the test {.center .pitfall-divider background-gradient="linear-gradient(160deg, #f7f4ef 0%, #f6e2c4 100%)"}

## Four questions, not one test {#sec-four-comparisons}

![Four cards: tests of whole distributions, stochastic superiority, specific features such as quantiles, and parametric parameters.](figures/sources/four-kinds-of-comparison.jpeg){fig-alt="Four panels. Whole empirical distributions ask whether two distribution functions are equal. Stochastic superiority asks whether one sample tends to be larger. Quantiles and scales ask about a named feature. Parametric tests ask about a parameter of a named distribution." width="88%"}

[Olszewski](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/adrianolszewski_there-exist-900-statistical-tests-many-share-7479152921432018944-tEK7/) groups comparisons of two or more samples by the question, from the most general to the most specific. About nine hundred named procedures sit in these groups. The name of the procedure is not the [hypothesis]{.mark}.

::: {.notes}
Read the four cards left to right as increasing specificity. "Nine hundred" is Olszewski's scale—use it to deflate test shopping. Ask which card a Mann–Whitney user actually picked (often not the one they think).
:::
## Whole distributions, then the tails

A test of the [empirical distribution functions]{.mark} asks only whether $F = G$. It does not say whether the difference is a shift, a scale, or a shape.

[Olszewski's family](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7413639530941091841/): Kolmogorov–Smirnov uses the largest vertical gap, and it is the least sensitive of the three. Cramér–von Mises integrates the squared gap, so a small gap that persists can count. Anderson–Darling uses the same integral with extra weight in the tails. For a heavy-tailed flux, Anderson–Darling is the one that looks where the mass of the question sits.

::: {.notes}
$F=G$ is the whole-distribution null—no location story yet. Compare KS (max gap), CvM (integrated gap), AD (tail-weighted). For heavy-tailed flux, name Anderson–Darling as the tail-aware member of the trio on the slide.

**Going further.** With empirical distribution functions $F_n$ and $G_m$ and the pooled $H_N$, Kolmogorov–Smirnov uses $\sup_t |F_n(t) - G_m(t)|$, Cramér–von Mises uses $\int (F_n - G_m)^2\, \mathrm{d}H_N$, and Anderson–Darling divides that integrand by $H_N(1 - H_N)$, which inflates the weight where $H_N$ is near 0 or 1. All three are distribution-free under $F = G$ for continuous data, so the null distribution does not depend on the shape; ties break that property and need a permutation null. Scholz and Stephens (*Journal of the American Statistical Association*, 1987) give the $k$-sample Anderson–Darling test.
:::
## A rank test is not a mean test

![Two examples. Left: equal medians, Mann–Whitney p below 0.001, and about 70 percent stochastic superiority. Right: medians differ by 10, Mann–Whitney p above 0.999, and stochastic superiority of 50 percent.](figures/sources/mann-whitney-not-a-median-test.jpeg){fig-alt="Left panel: two samples with the same median and Mann–Whitney p below 0.001, with about 70 percent of pairs ordered one way. Right panel: medians differ by 10, Mann–Whitney p above 0.999, and stochastic superiority of one half." width="78%"}

Mann–Whitney estimates $P(B>A)+\tfrac12 P(B=A)$. Equal medians can be decisive. A gap of 10 can be invisible. For a median, use [quantile regression](https://gist.github.com/adrianolszewski/2cec75678e1183e4703589bfd22fa8b2).

::: {.notes}
Left panel: equal medians, $p<0.001$, ~70% stochastic superiority. Right panel: medians differ by 10, $p>0.999$, 50% superiority. Read those numbers off the figure before defining the estimand. Mann–Whitney is not a median test—quantile regression is named for a median question.
:::
## Ranks answer a different question

Unless the two distributions differ only by a shift, a rank test mixes location, scale, and shape. Mann–Whitney can be small when the means are equal and the variances are not, and large when the means differ and the variances differ the other way. That is [Studentization]{.mark}: the null of a rank test is not the null of a mean.

If the planned question is a mean, stay with a procedure for a mean: a permutation Welch test, Freedman–Lane, or a wild bootstrap. Brunner–Munzel is the rank procedure that allows unequal variances, and it still estimates a probability, not $\mu$. The map of those choices is [the six columns](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/adrianolszewski_there-exist-900-statistical-tests-many-share-7479152921432018944-tEK7/).

::: {.notes}
Studentization is the keyword: rank null mixes location, scale, and shape. If the estimand is $\mu$, list permutation Welch, Freedman–Lane, wild bootstrap from the slide. Brunner–Munzel still targets a probability. Point to the six-column map link as the decision chart.

**Going further.** $U/(mn)$ is an unbiased estimator of $\theta = P(B > A) + \tfrac12 P(B = A)$, and the Mann–Whitney test is consistent only against alternatives with $\theta \ne \tfrac12$. Its permutation null assumes $F = G$, so with unequal variances and $\theta = \tfrac12$ the rejection rate is not $\alpha$. Brunner and Munzel (*Biometrical Journal*, 2000) studentise the estimate of $\theta$ with a rank-based variance, which makes the test asymptotically valid for $H_0: \theta = \tfrac12$ without $F = G$. Neither test is a test of means or medians unless one adds a shift model.
:::
## Six routes, one of them a mean

![Six columns of nonparametric comparisons: whole distributions, stochastic superiority, generalised locations, quantiles, robust mean-like estimators, and arithmetic means.](figures/sources/nonparametric-comparison-map.png){fig-alt="A diagram with six columns, from tests of the whole distribution, through ranks and quantiles, to permutation tests of an arithmetic mean." width="92%"}

The columns are questions. Mann–Whitney is the second, not a median. The last column is still a mean: permutation Welch, Freedman–Lane, a wild bootstrap.

::: {.notes}
Gesture across the six columns of the map image. Mann–Whitney lives in stochastic superiority, not the mean column. The last column is where permutation Welch and friends sit—keep that column in mind for the next slides.
:::
## Keep the mean, and change the standard error

![Table of ways to compare two means when variances differ, when there are outliers, or when the distribution is not Gaussian.](figures/sources/compare-means-no-covariate.png){fig-alt="A table. Equal variances: the ordinary t-test. Unequal variances: Welch. Outliers: Yuen or a robust regression, which changes the estimand to a trimmed or weighted mean. Non-Gaussian: a permutation or bootstrap t-test." width="86%"}

[Olszewski](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity/7445521856679407619/) keeps the mean when that is the question. Welch does not need a pretest of the variances. Yuen changes the target to a [trimmed mean]{.mark}. A permutation Welch test keeps the mean when the distribution is not Gaussian.

::: {.notes}
Read the table row by row: equal variances → ordinary $t$; unequal → Welch without an $F$ pretest; outliers → Yuen and a new estimand. The bottom row is permutation or bootstrap $t$ when the mean stays the question. Yuen is the row where the estimand quietly changes.

**Going further.** Two means with unequal variances is the Behrens–Fisher problem, which has no exact similar test. Welch's statistic $(\bar{Y}_1 - \bar{Y}_2)/\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1 + s_2^2/n_2}$ is referred to a $t$ with the Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom $\nu = (s_1^2/n_1 + s_2^2/n_2)^2 / \{s_1^4/(n_1^2(n_1 - 1)) + s_2^4/(n_2^2(n_2 - 1))\}$. When the variances are in fact equal it loses very little power, while the pooled test can be badly anti-conservative when the smaller group has the larger variance. Yuen's test applies the same construction to trimmed means and Winsorised variances (Wilcox, *Introduction to Robust Estimation and Hypothesis Testing*).
:::
## The same mean, with a covariate

![The lower half of the same table: ANCOVA by ordinary least squares, sandwich standard errors, generalised least squares, Freedman–Lane, and a wild bootstrap.](figures/sources/compare-means-with-covariate.png){fig-alt="Rows for a covariate-adjusted comparison of two means. Ordinary least squares when variances match and slopes are parallel. Sandwich standard errors or generalised least squares when variances differ. Freedman–Lane or a wild bootstrap when the distribution is not Gaussian." width="96%"}

Adding a covariate does not force a rank test. Ordinary least squares is the ANCOVA when the variances match and the slopes are parallel. Unequal variances move the standard error to a [sandwich estimator]{.mark} or to generalised least squares. A non-Gaussian residual moves the test to Freedman–Lane, or to a wild bootstrap, still for the mean.

::: {.notes}
This is the lower half of Olszewski's table—pair it mentally with the previous slide. ANCOVA by OLS needs parallel slopes and equal variance; sandwich or GLS relax variance; Freedman–Lane or wild bootstrap relax Gaussian residuals. The estimand remains a mean difference adjusted for the covariate.

**Going further.** The sandwich estimator $(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^{\top}\hat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})^{-1}$, with $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}} = \operatorname{diag}(e_i^2)$ (White, *Econometrica*, 1980), is consistent under heteroskedasticity of unknown form; the HC3 version divides $e_i^2$ by $(1 - h_{ii})^2$ and behaves better in small samples (MacKinnon and White, 1985). Freedman–Lane fits the reduced model without the treatment, permutes its residuals, adds them back to the reduced fit, and recomputes the full-model statistic (Freedman and Lane, 1983). The wild bootstrap multiplies each residual by an independent sign or a two-point weight, so each observation keeps its own variance (Wu, *Annals of Statistics*, 1986).
:::
## Prefer Welch when the model is this simple

![Side-by-side equivalence of a pooled t-test with ordinary least squares, and a Welch test with generalised least squares and Satterthwaite degrees of freedom.](figures/sources/welch-versus-ols-1.png){fig-alt="Two blocks. A pooled t-test matches a Wald test from ordinary least squares, estimate minus 2.99, p 0.049. A Welch test matches generalised least squares with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, the same estimate, p 0.052." width="72%"}

Start from Welch ([Olszewski](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7400680154634686464/)). The pooled test forces a common variance. In his sketch the estimate is $-2.99$ either way; the $p$-values are 0.049 and 0.052.

::: {.notes}
Same estimate $-2.99$, different $p$: 0.049 pooled versus 0.052 Welch. Use that pair to show the decision is in the standard error, not the contrast. Pooled $t$ equals homoscedastic OLS; Welch equals GLS with Satterthwaite df on the figure.
:::
## A permutation $p$ for the same Welch statistic {#sec-perm-welch}

[Olszewski](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7490552621573922816/): `MKinfer::perm.t.test` uses the Welch–Satterthwaite statistic unless you set `var.equal = TRUE`. Leave the default. Do not pretest the variances with an $F$ test.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
result <- MKinfer::perm.t.test(
  response ~ group, data = data, permStat = TRUE
)
MKinfer::h0plot(result)
```

::: {.notes}
The call returns the classical $p$ and the permutation $p$. Compare them, and look at the null distribution of the permuted statistic as well as the residual QQ plot. Use more than 9999 draws for a stable $p$, and on the order of 50,000 if the level of interest is below 0.001. Record the seed. Permuting the raw difference of means quietly assumes equal variances. The studentized statistic is the one Janssen (1997) gives for unequal variances; he lists that paper under the post. A reported permutation $p$ of exactly 0 is a convention about the draws, not a probability.

**Going further.** A permutation test is exact when the observations are exchangeable under the null; equal means with unequal variances do not give exchangeability. Chung and Romano (*Annals of Statistics*, 2013) show that permuting a studentised statistic gives a test that is exact under exchangeability and asymptotically valid under the weaker mean null, which is why the Welch statistic is the one to permute. With $B$ random permutations, report $(1 + \#\{T^*_b \ge T\})/(1 + B)$, which is never 0 and keeps the test valid (Phipson and Smyth, *Statistical Applications in Genetics and Molecular Biology*, 2010).
:::

## Compare the two $p$-values, then the null plot

`h0plot()` on the same object shows the permuted statistic under the null beside the two $p$-values on the printout. If the classical and permutation $p$ disagree, the Gaussian approximation was doing work.

::: {.notes}
This slide is only the picture. The draw count, seed, and Welch-versus-raw permutation point are on the previous slide's notes. Thirty seconds.
:::

## A bell curve is not a feature test {#sec-meaningless-sigma}

![Recovery rates piled against 100 percent, with a 1-sigma interval of 92 plus or minus 12 and a 2-sigma interval of 92 plus or minus 24, beside a normal bell marked 68, 95, and 99.7 percent.](figures/sources/egu-recovery-two-sigma.png){fig-alt="Histogram of percent area recovered within 30 years, piled at 100 percent. A 1-sigma band of 92 plus or minus 12 stays inside 0 to 100. A 2-sigma band of 92 plus or minus 24 does not. A Gaussian bell sits beside the histogram." width="92%"}

[Hartmann and Rudolph](https://github.com/soga-lab/EGU2026_SC). The 2-sigma interval is 92 ± 24%, so it leaves 0–100. The bell beside it is the 68%, 95%, 99.7% picture. A normality test does not turn that interval into a recovery rate. The same objection applies to a concentration, a count, or a composition.

::: {.notes}
Point at the histogram piled at 100% and the 92 ± 24% band leaving the 0–100 scale. The bell's 68/95/99.7 labels are the wrong feature for bounded recovery. A normality test on such data does not repair the interval—shape and support are separate failures.
:::
## The excuse is not a diagnosis

The same slides list the defences of that summary:

- everybody reports it this way
- the variance was large
- $n$ was too small for anything more accurate
- it is the reporting standard
- one only wanted the mean and the variability
- the statistically careful version made the story disappear

None of these is a reason to attach a Gaussian spread to a feature whose scale forbids it. The [QQ plot](#sec-qq-read) shows the shape. It does not choose the [summary]{.mark}.

::: {.notes}
Read two or three excuses from the bullet list and invite the room to name others they have heard. Close with the QQ plot link: diagnosis of shape is not the same as choosing a summary on the right scale. Keep the tone practical, not preachy.
:::
## A transform changes the question {.center .pitfall-divider background-gradient="linear-gradient(160deg, #f7f4ef 0%, #e4d8f5 100%)"}

## Before you transform $Y$

Write two answers, and keep them.

1. Why is transforming the response usually a bad default?
2. What do you do instead when a Gaussian model for $Y$ does not fit?

[Olszewski's](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/why-transforming-response-regression-analysis-testing-olszewski/) answers, from the 2022 note, follow the variance-stabilising case. A multiplicative process is the case he keeps. A skewed histogram is not.

::: {.notes}
Pause on the two numbered questions—let someone answer before you advance. Olszewski's "bad default" is about rewriting the estimand without science; the alternative is a model matched to $Y$. Skew alone is not on his justification list.
:::
## A transformation can be the right scale

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
A transform is justified when it matches the science:

- a [multiplicative]{.mark} effect, so that logs are the natural contrast
- a variance that grows with the mean, and a log that stabilises it
- a physical rate that is already defined on a log scale
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
![](figures/generated/sketch-nongauss-a-log-ruler.png){.sketch fig-alt="A ruler marked 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 at equal spacing, with a green arrow labelled times 2 between each pair of ticks."}
:::
::::

It is not justified by "the histogram looked skewed" alone. What that shortcut costs starts at [a transform rewrites the question](#sec-transform-rewrite).

::: {.notes}
Walk the three justified bullets: multiplicative effects, variance growing with mean, physical log scale. The closing sentence is the guardrail—histogram skew is not on the list. Link to the transform-rewrite slide for the cost of ignoring that guardrail.
:::
## Match the transform to $v(\mu)$ {#sec-vst}

[Huber, chapter 13](https://www.huber.embl.de/msmb/13-chap.html#mean-variance-relationships-and-variance-stabilizing-transformations), writes $v(\mu)$ for the way the variance trends with the mean. Three prototypes cover most assays:

- constant: $v(\mu) = c$
- Poisson-like: $v(\mu) = a\mu$
- quadratic: the standard deviation proportional to the mean, so $v(\mu) = b\mu^2$

A real measurement can add them. For microarray fluorescence he cites Rocke and Durbin (2001): background plus a multiplicative noise, $v(\mu) = b\mu^2 + c$. A [variance-stabilising transformation]{.mark} is built from that curve, so replicate spread no longer tracks the mean. One power for the whole sample, as on the [Yeo–Johnson slide](#sec-yeo), does not use $v(\mu)$.

::: {.notes}
Huber's three prototypes—constant, Poisson-like $a\mu$, quadratic $b\mu^2$—are the vocabulary. Rocke–Durbin adds $b\mu^2+c$ as a realistic assay. Contrast VST built from $v(\mu)$ with Yeo–Johnson chasing a bell shape for the whole column.

**Going further.** The delta method gives $\operatorname{Var}\{f(Y)\} \approx f'(\mu)^2 v(\mu)$, so the stabilising choice solves $f'(\mu) \propto v(\mu)^{-1/2}$, that is $f(\mu) = \int^{\mu} v(t)^{-1/2}\, \mathrm{d}t$. Constant $v$ gives the identity, $v = a\mu$ gives $\sqrt{\mu}$ (Anscombe's $\sqrt{Y + 3/8}$ refines it for Poisson counts), $v = b\mu^2$ gives $\log \mu$, and $v = b\mu^2 + c$ gives an inverse hyperbolic sine, the generalised log of Huber and colleagues (*Bioinformatics*, 2002). The approximation is first order: it is poor for small counts, where the variance of $f(Y)$ still depends on $\mu$.
:::
## A VST is for a Euclidean next step {#sec-vst-pca}

Reasons for analysing the transformed scale:

::: {.incremental}
- a plot, or a heatmap, that spends its ink across the range

- PCA, or a clustering that uses correlation, no longer dominated by a few very large means

- a method that assumes identical, homoskedastic noise
:::


That is the machine-learning case: a method whose geometry is [Euclidean]{.mark} and wants a roughly constant spread. The transformation is still a new response. Inference for $\mu$ on the original support stays with the [link](#sec-glm-versus-transform).

::: {.notes}
Step the three fragments: heatmaps, PCA dominated by large means, homoskedastic noise for ML. VST is a preprocessing choice for geometry, not automatic inference on the original scale. The link at the end points to GLMs as the inference path.

**Going further.** DESeq2's `vst()` integrates the fitted dispersion trend $v(\mu) = \mu + \alpha(\mu)\mu^2$ of the negative binomial, and `rlog()` shrinks each gene's log fold changes towards zero with an empirical prior (Love, Huber, and Anders, *Genome Biology*, 2014). Both are meant for distances, clustering, and plots; the differential test itself is done on the counts with the negative binomial likelihood. A Euclidean distance on the transformed scale is then close to a distance that gives each gene a comparable noise level.
:::

## Five count transforms {#sec-count-transforms .smaller}

| Transform | Equation | Suited to | Trade-off |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| VST | $\mathrm{Var}\{f(Y)\} \approx c$ | PCA, heatmaps | ✅ low counts · ❌ not a test of $\mu$ |
| rlog | $\log$ with shrinkage at low counts | PCA, small $n$ | ✅ stable · ❌ can compress a real difference |
| $\log_2(\mathrm{CPM}+c)$ | $\log_2(10^6 Y/N + c)$ | a quick heatmap | ✅ fast · ❌ $c$ is arbitrary |
| voom | $\log_2\mathrm{CPM}$, plus a weight | a linear model after | ✅ models the spread · ❌ the weight is the point |
| CLR | $\log(x_j / g(x))$ | a composition | ✅ scale-free · ❌ zeros need a rule |

$g(x)$ is the geometric mean within the sample. $N$ is the library size. None of these is a replacement for a [link on $\mu$](#sec-glm-versus-transform).

::: {.notes}
Read the trade-off column, not every equation. CLR is the composition row. VST and rlog are for a Euclidean next step, which is the previous slide. Do not recommend one of them for a rate ratio.

**Going further.** The centred log-ratio maps a composition $x$ with $D$ parts to $\log\{x_j / g(x)\}$, which sums to zero, so its covariance matrix is singular; the isometric log-ratio (Egozcue and colleagues, *Mathematical Geology*, 2003) gives $D - 1$ orthonormal coordinates instead. Aitchison, *The Statistical Analysis of Compositional Data* (1986), is the foundation. voom estimates a smooth mean–variance trend of $\log_2\mathrm{CPM}$ and turns it into precision weights for each observation, so limma's weighted least squares inherits $v(\mu)$ (Law and colleagues, *Genome Biology*, 2014).
:::
## A transform rewrites the question {#sec-transform-rewrite}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
A logarithm changes a difference of arithmetic means into a ratio of [geometric means]{.mark}. A Box–Cox power such as $-0.67$ is not a unit anyone measured.

On $\log Y$ against $x$, a small coefficient is nearly a percentage: $\exp(0.05) \approx 1.05$. A coefficient of $0.5$ is not a 50% change, because $\exp(0.5) \approx 1.65$. The inequality that separates the two means is [written later](#sec-log-estimand).
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
![](figures/generated/sketch-nongauss-a-exp-coef.png){.sketch fig-alt="Two curves against beta: the blue line 1 plus beta and the red curve exp of beta. They touch near 0.05 and a red arrow marks the gap at 0.5."}
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Box–Cox power $-0.67$ is the absurd unit example. Contrast $\exp(0.05)\approx 1.05$ with $\exp(0.5)\approx 1.65$ so students stop saying "0.5 on the log is 50%". Forward to the log-estimand inequality slide.

**Going further.** On $\log Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \varepsilon$, a one-unit change in $x$ multiplies the geometric mean, and the median when $\varepsilon$ is symmetric, by $e^{\beta_1}$, a change of $100(e^{\beta_1} - 1)\%$. Box and Cox (*Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B*, 1964) choose $\lambda$ in $(Y^{\lambda} - 1)/\lambda$ by profile likelihood. Inference on $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ treating $\hat{\lambda}$ as known understates the uncertainty, and $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ has no fixed meaning across $\lambda$; Bickel and Doksum (1981) and the reply by Box and Cox (1982) are the classic exchange on that point.
:::
## The variance travels with the mean

In a Gaussian model the mean and the variance are separate parameters. After a log they are [tied]{.mark}: a log-normal variance depends on the mean. A power chosen only to stabilise the spread changes that relationship even when the power is not a logarithm.

::: {.notes}
Gaussian $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$ separate; log-normal ties them. Any power transform for stabilisation also couples mean and spread—even when it is not $\log$. One sentence slide: do not rush.

**Going further.** If $\log Y \sim \mathcal{N}(m, s^2)$, then $\mathbb{E}(Y) = \mu = e^{m + s^2/2}$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Y) = (e^{s^2} - 1)\mu^2$. A constant variance on the log scale is therefore a constant coefficient of variation, $v(\mu) \propto \mu^2$, on the original scale. The same variance function belongs to the gamma family, so a gamma GLM with a log link targets $\mathbb{E}(Y \mid \mathbf{x})$ directly with that mean–variance relation (McCullagh and Nelder, *Generalized Linear Models*, 1989, chapter 8).
:::
## The interval does not travel back

For a [convex]{.mark} $f$,

$$
f\!\left(\mathbb{E}[Y]\right) \le \mathbb{E}[f(Y)].
$$ {#eq-jensen}

The two sides meet when $f$ is linear. A confidence interval, a moment, or a test computed on $f(Y)$ is not the same object on the original scale after $f^{-1}$. The log case is the [estimand slide](#sec-log-estimand). @eq-jensen is why.

::: {.notes}
Read @eq-jensen once. The next slide draws the gap. A common misread is to invert a CI on $f(Y)$ and call it a CI for $\mathbb{E}(Y)$.

**Going further.** Jensen's inequality holds for any convex $f$ and integrable $Y$, with equality if and only if $f$ is affine on the support of $Y$ or $Y$ is degenerate. A second-order expansion gives the size of the gap: $\mathbb{E}\{f(Y)\} \approx f(\mu) + \tfrac12 f''(\mu)\operatorname{Var}(Y)$. What does travel back is a quantile: for a monotone $f$, $f^{-1}$ of a quantile of $f(Y)$ is the same quantile of $Y$. So an interval for the mean of $\log Y$, back-transformed, is an interval for the median of $Y$ when $\log Y$ is symmetric, not for its mean.
:::

## Convex pulls the mean up {.smaller #sec-jensen-shapes}

![Left, a convex curve with the chord above it and an arrow for the Jensen gap. Right, a concave curve with the gap running the other way.](figures/generated/jensen-convex-concave.png){fig-alt="Two panels. Left, y squared, convex: the average of the function sits above the function of the average, with an upward arrow for the gap. Right, the logarithm, concave: the gap runs downward." width="96%"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Convex**, such as $y^2$.

The green point is $f(\mathbb{E}[Y])$. The red point is $\mathbb{E}[f(Y)]$. The arrow is the gap in @eq-jensen.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Concave**, such as $\log y$.

The inequality reverses. Back-transforming a mean on the log scale lands off $\mathbb{E}(Y)$.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Point at the arrow, not the curve. Convex: the average of $f(Y)$ sits above $f$ of the average. Concave, including the log: the gap runs the other way, which is the back-transformed mean.
:::

## A logarithm needs a positive response

$\log Y$ is undefined when $Y$ can be negative. Adding a constant, as in $\log(Y + c)$, defines a [different response]{.mark}. A bone-density T-score is one measurement that is allowed to be negative. Quantile regression does not need the sign. Yeo–Johnson is the power that allows negatives, and the [later slide](#sec-yeo) says what that power costs.

![](figures/generated/sketch-nongauss-a-log-domain.png){.sketch fig-alt="A red hatched region labelled Y at most 0 with log and a question mark, beside a blue log curve that exists only for positive Y." fig-align="center"}

::: {.notes}
$\log(Y+c)$ is a new response, not a fix for negatives. T-score is the named example of legitimate negative $Y$. Quantile regression and Yeo–Johnson are the two exits named on the slide—different estimands, different costs.

**Going further.** Box–Cox is defined only for $Y > 0$; the two-parameter version $(Y + c)^{\lambda}$ makes $c$ a parameter whose value changes the estimand. The inverse hyperbolic sine, $\operatorname{asinh}(Y) = \log(Y + \sqrt{Y^2 + 1})$, accepts zeros and negatives but its coefficients depend on the units of $Y$ (Bellemare and Wichman, *Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics*, 2020). For non-negative $Y$ with exact zeros, a Tweedie or a hurdle model keeps the mean on the original scale.
:::

## The hypothesis moved {#sec-transform-hypothesis}

A log is meaningful when the question was a ratio of geometric means, or a difference of means on a multiplicative scale.

- A power such as $-0.67$ does not name a new question
- Volume and a cube root, or a speed and $1/y$, can name one
- Rank tests such as Mann–Whitney also change the question, to [stochastic superiority]{.mark}, and that is not a mean unless the two samples are identical in shape

🔗 [Adrian Olszewski](https://www.2kmm.pl/blog/On-the-ubiquity-of-skewness-in-nature/) states the point as a change of hypothesis. 📄 [Pek, Wong, and Wong (2018)](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2018.02104) review the same split: transform the data, or leave $Y$ and change the inference.

::: {.notes}
Ask what hypothesis $\lambda = -0.67$ tests. The honest answer is that nobody wrote it down. Pek is the review; do not open the taxonomy. One minute.
:::

## The mean and the variance are tied {#sec-transform-variance}

Transforming the column changes how the spread sits on the mean.

- In a GLM the link acts on $\mu$, and the variance stays a function of that $\mu$
- A power applied to $Y$ rewrites both

::: {.notes}
A GLM moves $\mu$. A power moves the column, so the mean and the spread move together. One minute.
:::

## The conditionals were already fine {#sec-transform-conditional}

A marginal histogram can look skewed because several Gaussian groups, with different means, were [pooled]{.mark}.

- Each conditional $Y \mid x$ can already be Gaussian
- Transforming the pooled column rewrites those conditionals
- The picture is [the pooled histogram](#sec-pooled-histogram)

![](figures/generated/sketch-nongauss-a-pooled-bells.png){.sketch fig-alt="Two green bell curves for two groups, an arrow, and a red right-skewed histogram labelled pooled." fig-align="center"}

::: {.notes}
Ask them to imagine two normal groups with different means, stacked into one histogram. The skew is the mixture. Transforming that mixture is not a repair of either group.

**Going further.** The marginal density is a mixture, $f(y) = \sum_k w_k\, \varphi\{(y - \mu_k)/\sigma\}/\sigma$, and by the law of total variance $\operatorname{Var}(Y) = \mathbb{E}\{\operatorname{Var}(Y \mid x)\} + \operatorname{Var}\{\mathbb{E}(Y \mid x)\}$. The marginal skewness comes entirely from the spread of the conditional means and the weights. A transformation chosen on $f(y)$ therefore reacts to the design, not to the error distribution the model assumes.
:::

## Back-transformation misses the mean {#sec-transform-back}

@eq-jensen is the gap. Inverting a fit on the Box–Cox scale does not return $\mathbb{E}(Y \mid x)$.

📄 [Gonçalves (2026)](https://doi.org/10.3390/axioms15070519) shows that conditional expectation and the inverse Box–Cox transform do not [commute]{.mark}. The inverse-transformed curve is not, in general, the conditional mean on the original scale.

![](figures/generated/sketch-nongauss-a-not-commute.png){.sketch-sm fig-alt="A square of arrows. Y averaged gives E of Y in green. Y logged, averaged, then exponentiated arrives in red beside E of Y with a not-equal sign." fig-align="center"}

::: {.notes}
One sentence from the abstract is enough: expectation and inversion do not commute. Do not derive the truncated-normal correction.

**Going further.** If $\log Y = \mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon$ independent of $\mathbf{x}$, then $\mathbb{E}(Y \mid \mathbf{x}) = e^{\mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}}\, \mathbb{E}(e^{\varepsilon})$. Under a Gaussian $\varepsilon$ that factor is $e^{\sigma^2/2}$; without the Gaussian assumption, Duan's smearing estimator replaces it by $n^{-1}\sum_i e^{e_i}$ (Duan, *Journal of the American Statistical Association*, 1983). Both corrections fail when $\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon \mid \mathbf{x})$ depends on $\mathbf{x}$, because the factor then varies with $\mathbf{x}$ and the retransformed slopes are biased (Manning, *Journal of Health Economics*, 1998). A GLM with a log link avoids the retransformation altogether.
:::

## A transform is not a guarantee {#sec-transform-normal}

A power chosen to look more Gaussian does not deliver Gaussian residuals.

- The histogram can still be skewed
- The hypothesis is no longer the one that was asked
- For a prediction, a transform can still be a useful scale
- For an inference, the result has to be a quantity you can say in the units of $Y$

Permutation and bootstrap procedures that keep $Y$ are the alternative when the question was a mean. Quantile regression is the alternative when you accept a different, named question.

::: {.notes}
Close Adrian's list on the fourth and fifth points: Jensen was the previous slide, and normality is not guaranteed. Prediction may still use a transform. Inference has to name the new question. Forty seconds.
:::

## The pooled histogram is the wrong picture {#sec-pooled-histogram}

Conditional Gaussian groups with different means look skewed once you pool them. In his sketch the groups are normal, seed 1000, and the model is `lm(DV ~ IV)`. Logging the pooled $Y$ because the histogram is skewed spoils residuals that were already close to Gaussian.

Transform when the **conditional** distribution is skewed. That is what the residual plot checks. If $\mathbb{E}(Y \mid x)$ is already approximately Gaussian, the transform is not the remedy.

::: {.notes}
Olszewski's sketch: normal groups, different means, pooled skew. Logging pooled $Y$ can wreck residuals that were fine conditional on `IV`. Seed 1000 and `lm(DV ~ IV)` are on the slide—illustrative. Conditional versus marginal is the whole point.

**Going further.** Under the model $Y_i = \mu(x_i) + \varepsilon_i$ with Gaussian errors, the residuals $Y_i - \hat{\mu}(x_i)$ are approximately Gaussian while the pooled $Y_i$ follow a mixture whose shape is set by the design. A transformation such as $\log$ applied to the pooled $Y$ is a nonlinear function of $\mu(x_i) + \varepsilon_i$, so the transformed errors are no longer additive or identically distributed across groups. Box–Cox's own likelihood is conditional on $x$, which is why profiling $\lambda$ in `MASS::boxcox(lm(y ~ x))` and on `y` alone can give very different powers.
:::
## The centre has to match the scale {#sec-scales}

```{r}
#| echo: false
math <- function(tex) gt::html(sprintf('<span class="math inline">\\(%s\\)</span>', tex))

scales <- data.frame(
  Scale = c(
    "Binomial", "Nominal", "Ordinal", "Interval",
    "Rational", "Logistic", "Concentration"
  ),
  Measure = I(c(
    "Success or failure",
    "Category membership",
    math("\\text{ordered by } <"),
    math("d=|x_1-x_2|"),
    math("x_1/x_2"),
    math("(x-l)/(u-x)"),
    "Part of a constant sum"
  )),
  Example = c(
    "Rainy days", "Soil types", "Hurricane category",
    "Time, location", "Length, weight, isotope ratio",
    "Elevation, depth", "TOC, recovery rate"
  ),
  Similarity = c(
    "Equality only", "Equality", "Rank order",
    "Additive, near 0", "Multiplicative, near 1",
    "Log-ratio", "Aitchison distance"
  ),
  Centre = I(c(
    math("np"),
    math("\\text{mode, }\\bar{x}_{\\mathrm{geo}},\\, np_i"),
    math("Q_{50}"),
    "Arithmetic mean",
    "Geometric mean",
    "Logistic mean",
    "Geometric mean"
  )),
  Spread = I(c(
    math("np(1-p)"),
    "Entropy",
    math("Q_{75}-Q_{25}"),
    "Arithmetic sd",
    "Geometric sd",
    "Logistic variance",
    "Compositional variance"
  )),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

scales |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::tab_options(
    table.font.size = "15px",
    data_row.padding = gt::px(2),
    column_labels.font.size = "15px"
  )
```

[Hartmann and Rudolph](https://github.com/soga-lab/EGU2026_SC). An arithmetic mean is the interval row. A ratio wants a [geometric mean]{.mark}. TOC and a recovery are parts of a sum, not interval measurements.

::: {.notes}
Walk the gt table row by row: Interval → arithmetic mean; Rational → geometric; Concentration → geometric on parts of a sum. Hartmann and Rudolph's TOC and recovery examples are compositional, not interval. Ask which centre matches an isotope ratio versus a recovery rate.
:::
## A constant sum is a simplex

If the parts add to a constant, the point is not free in the plane. The picture: $x + y = 1$ is a line segment, not a square. A sequencing library is the same constraint. The counts in one sample add to the library size, so a gene is a [share]{.mark} of that sum. A Gaussian interval on the count, or on a shifted logarithm of the count, does not respect it.

![](figures/generated/sketch-nongauss-a-simplex.png){.sketch fig-alt="A grey square with its red diagonal x plus y equals 1; three red points sit on the diagonal." fig-align="center"}

::: {.notes}
Use $x+y=1$ as the line-segment picture before sequencing. Library size fixes the sum of counts; a gene share lives on a simplex. Gaussian intervals on raw counts ignore that constraint—preview compositional methods without opening the full chapter.

**Going further.** Closure, dividing each part by the total, induces negative bias in the correlations between parts: for $D$ parts with constant sum, the covariances in each row of the covariance matrix sum to zero. Pearson called this spurious correlation in 1897. Aitchison's log-ratio geometry makes the simplex a Euclidean space, in which distances and means are invariant to the arbitrary total. For sequencing counts, Gloor and colleagues (*Frontiers in Microbiology*, 2017) argue that this treatment is not optional, because the library size carries no biological information.
:::
## Five steps that rewrite $Y$

For a positive $x$, a common checklist is:

- inspect a histogram, a box plot, or a QQ plot
- if the lower limit is positive, add a constant
- take $\log x$ and check that the logs look more Gaussian
- average the logs and take their standard deviation
- exponentiate both, and report the geometric mean times or divided by the [geometric standard deviation]{.mark}

They note that this interval stays positive. That is not the same as an interval for $\mathbb{E}(Y)$.

::: {.notes}
Read the five-step checklist aloud once. The slide's own caveat is the punchline: positivity of the reported interval is not an interval for $\mathbb{E}(Y)$. Students recognise this pipeline from papers; name what estimand the geometric mean times/divided by GSD actually targets.
:::
## The exponential does not return the moment

$\exp(\overline{\log x})$ is the geometric mean. It is not $\mathbb{E}(Y)$. Exponentiating the standard deviation of the logs does not return the standard deviation of $Y$. A shift before the logarithm is a third response. The [inequality](#sec-log-estimand) is why the two means differ. Prefer a model for $\mu$, or a robust summary, over this sequence.

::: {.notes}
$\exp(\overline{\log x})$ is the geometric mean, not $\mathbb{E}(Y)$. Exponentiating the log SD is not the SD on the original scale. Shift before log is a third response—link to the log-estimand inequality slide.

**Going further.** If $\log Y \sim \mathcal{N}(m, s^2)$, the geometric mean is $e^{m}$, the geometric standard deviation is $e^{s}$, the mean is $e^{m + s^2/2}$, and the standard deviation is $e^{m + s^2/2}\sqrt{e^{s^2} - 1}$. The interval $e^{m} \times\!/ e^{2s}$ covers about 95% of $Y$, which is a prediction interval for an observation, not a confidence interval for $\mathbb{E}(Y)$. Estimating $\mathbb{E}(Y)$ from logged data needs $s^2$ and, for small samples, the unbiased estimator of Finney (*Supplement to the Journal of the Royal Statistical Society*, 1941).
:::
## A logit link stays inside the bounds

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
For a recovery, or any proportion, model $\operatorname{logit}(\pi)$ with $\pi = \mathbb{E}(Y \mid x)$. When $Y$ is binary this is logistic regression. The same link is the model for a proportion. The reported interval is the [inverse logit]{.mark} of the interval for the linear predictor. It stays in $(0, 1)$, and the test is a test of $\pi$.
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
![](figures/generated/sketch-nongauss-a-logit-bounds.png){.sketch fig-alt="Dashed bounds at 0 and 1. A red straight line crosses both and is marked wrong; a green S-curve stays between them and is marked pi."}
:::
::::

It is not the arithmetic mean of a column that was transformed until a QQ plot looked straight.

::: {.notes}
Model $\operatorname{logit}(\pi)$ with $\pi=\mathbb{E}(Y\mid x)$; inverse logit intervals stay in $(0,1)$. Contrast with transforming a column until a QQ plot looks straight—that is not a test of $\pi$. Binary and proportion cases share the same link sentence on the slide.

**Going further.** With a known denominator $m_i$, a proportion is $Y_i/m_i$ with $Y_i \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(m_i, \pi_i)$, fitted with `cbind(successes, failures)` or `weights = m`. Without a denominator, Papke and Wooldridge (*Journal of Applied Econometrics*, 1996) use the binomial quasi-likelihood: the estimating equation needs only $\mathbb{E}(Y \mid \mathbf{x}) = \operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta})$, and a sandwich standard error covers the variance. Beta regression adds a full likelihood for $Y \in (0, 1)$ (Ferrari and Cribari-Neto, *Journal of Applied Statistics*, 2004); exact 0s and 1s need a zero- or one-inflated version.
:::
## Put the curve in $\mu$, not in $Y$

A nonlinear regression lets $\mu$ be a nonlinear function of $x$. A generalised linear model leaves $Y$ alone and puts a [link]{.mark} on $\mu$. Both keep the original response. The link is the rest of this hour, from the [skeleton](#sec-skeleton).

::: {.notes}
Nonlinear regression bends $\mu(x)$; GLM bends $g(\mu)$ while $Y$ stays on its support. Both keep the measured response. Point to the skeleton slide as the next hour's route map.

**Going further.** A nonlinear model $Y_i = m(\mathbf{x}_i; \boldsymbol{\theta}) + \varepsilon_i$ is fitted by Gauss–Newton least squares, which is maximum likelihood under additive Gaussian errors; its inference relies on a local linearisation whose accuracy depends on the curvature of the model (Bates and Watts, *Nonlinear Regression Analysis and Its Applications*, 1988). A GLM is the special case where $m = g^{-1}(\mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta})$ and the error law comes from the family, not from an additive Gaussian term. Both keep $\mathbb{E}(Y \mid \mathbf{x})$ as the target.
:::
## Or model the variance, or change the summary

::: {.incremental}
- [Generalised least squares or estimating equations](#sec-ols-replacements) when the variance or the correlation is the problem, and the mean is still the target.

- [Quantile regression]{.mark} when the target is a quantile, including a median, and including censored $Y$.

- A robust or rank procedure when the question is not an arithmetic mean. The [map](#sec-four-comparisons) is that choice. A [permutation Welch test](#sec-perm-welch) is the choice when the mean remains the question.
:::


::: {.notes}
Step the three fragments: GLS/GEE for variance structure; quantile regression for a quantile estimand; robust/rank or permutation Welch when the mean is not the question. The four-comparisons map is the routing table for fragment three.

**Going further.** Generalised estimating equations solve $\sum_j \mathbf{D}_j^{\top}\mathbf{V}_j^{-1}(\mathbf{Y}_j - \boldsymbol{\mu}_j) = \mathbf{0}$ over clusters $j$, with a working correlation inside $\mathbf{V}_j$; Liang and Zeger (*Biometrika*, 1986) show that $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ is consistent and the sandwich variance valid even when that working correlation is wrong, provided the mean model is right and the number of clusters is large. Quantile regression minimises $\sum_i \rho_\tau(Y_i - \mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta})$ with the check loss $\rho_\tau(u) = u\{\tau - \mathbb{1}(u < 0)\}$ (Koenker and Bassett, *Econometrica*, 1978); it needs no distributional assumption on $Y \mid \mathbf{x}$ and is equivariant under monotone transformations.
:::
## $\log Y$ changes the estimand {#sec-log-estimand}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
A Gaussian model for $\log Y$ targets $\mathbb{E}(\log Y \mid x)$.

$$
\exp\{\mathbb{E}(\log Y \mid x)\} \le \mathbb{E}(Y \mid x),
$$

with equality only in degenerate cases. The left-hand side behaves like a geometric mean. The right-hand side is the arithmetic mean on the original scale.
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
![](figures/generated/sketch-nongauss-a-gm-am.png){.sketch fig-alt="A right-skewed density with a red vertical line at exp of E of log Y and, to its right, a green vertical line at E of Y."}
:::
::::

$\log(Y+1)$ is a [third response]{.mark}. Zeros were the reason for the $+1$, and they are still in the model, only hidden.

For counts, start from a distribution on the non-negative integers ([O'Hara and Kotze, 2010](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2041-210X.2010.00021.x); [@agrestiFoundationsLinearGeneralized2015]).

::: {.notes}
Read the inequality: $\exp\{\mathbb{E}(\log Y\mid x)\}\le \mathbb{E}(Y\mid x)$. $\log(Y+1)$ hides zeros but changes the response again. Close with counts needing an integer model—O'Hara and Kotze on the slide.

**Going further.** Under $\log Y = \mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ independent of $\mathbf{x}$, $\mathbb{E}(Y \mid \mathbf{x}) = \exp(\mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \sigma^2/2)$. Ratios of arithmetic means are then also $e^{\beta_1}$, so the slope survives; only the level is biased. That rescue fails as soon as $\sigma^2$ depends on $\mathbf{x}$, which is the usual situation for counts. O'Hara and Kotze (2010) show by simulation that $\log(Y + 1)$ followed by least squares gives biased estimates for counts with low means, where a Poisson or negative binomial GLM does not.
:::
## Powers that chase a Gaussian shape {#sec-yeo}

Yeo–Johnson chooses a power, including for zeros and negative values, so that the transformed sample is closer to Gaussian. When the next method is Euclidean, such as a PCA, the transform that follows $v(\mu)$ is the [variance-stabilising transformation](#sec-vst).

- the criterion is closeness to a [bell shape]{.mark}, not a scientific unit
- the inverse transform is awkward, so a mean on the transformed scale is hard to say in the original unit
- if you use it, describe the original $Y$ with the median and the quartiles

It does not replace a likelihood whose support is the support of $Y$.

::: {.notes}
Yeo–Johnson optimises toward Gaussianity for PCA-like steps, not toward a scientific unit. If used, report median and quartiles on original $Y$. VST from $v(\mu)$ is the principled alternative named in the first bullet's cross-link.

**Going further.** Yeo and Johnson (*Biometrika*, 2000) define $\psi(y, \lambda) = \{(y + 1)^{\lambda} - 1\}/\lambda$ for $y \ge 0$ and $-\{(1 - y)^{2 - \lambda} - 1\}/(2 - \lambda)$ for $y < 0$, with logarithmic limits at $\lambda = 0$ and $\lambda = 2$, and choose $\lambda$ by maximising a Gaussian likelihood. The criterion is symmetry of the marginal sample, so the chosen $\lambda$ changes with the mix of covariate values in the data. The transform is continuous and monotone, so quantiles back-transform exactly, which is why the median and quartiles remain interpretable while a mean does not.
:::
## A test is a model with one factor {#sec-tests-as-linear}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
[Lindeløv](https://lindeloev.github.io/tests-as-linear/) writes the common tests as linear models. A Pearson correlation is the slope in `lm(scale(y) ~ scale(x))`: standardising both variables makes that slope equal to $r$. A $\chi^2$ test of counts is a [Poisson log-linear model]{.mark}, `glm(counts ~ group, family = poisson)`, compared with an intercept-only model.
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
![](figures/generated/sketch-nongauss-a-test-as-line.png){.sketch fig-alt="Blue points for group 0 and group 1 joined by a red line between the group means, labelled slope equals difference."}
:::
::::

The model is the more flexible object. It keeps the same contrast and adds a covariate, a variance weight, or a link. A named test usually cannot.

::: {.notes}
Pearson $r$ as `lm(scale(y)~scale(x))` and $\chi^2$ as Poisson `glm(counts~group)` are the two Lindeløv examples. The model generalises with covariates, weights, and links; the named test often does not.

**Going further.** Pearson's $X^2 = \sum (O - E)^2/E$ is the score test of the Poisson log-linear model of independence against the saturated model, and the likelihood-ratio statistic $G^2 = 2\sum O \log(O/E)$ is its deviance; both are asymptotically $\chi^2$ with the same degrees of freedom. The Poisson and multinomial likelihoods give the same estimates for the interaction terms once the margins are fitted, which is why the sampling scheme does not change the test (Agresti, *Categorical Data Analysis*). The approximation needs expected counts that are not too small, the usual rule being about 5.
:::
## A paired $t$ reports the mean

[Loïc](https://statsxomics.blog/2024/05/25/why-you-should-use-regression-models-instead-of-tests-for-statistical-inferences/), seed 1234, 100 people measured twice. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test gives $V = 1711$ and $p = 0.005$. The paired $t$ test gives a mean difference of $-0.42$, an interval from $-0.69$ to $-0.14$, and $p = 0.003$. The sign is the order of the two levels.

Both reject. Only the paired $t$ test says how large the mean change is. The signed-rank test is a statement about the ranks of the within-person differences.

::: {.notes}
Wilcoxon $V=1711$, $p=0.005$ versus paired $t$ mean difference $-0.42$ with interval $-0.69$ to $-0.14$, $p=0.003$, seed 1234. Both reject; only the $t$ states how large the mean shift is. Signed-rank is about ranks of within-person differences.
:::
## The pair is a random intercept

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
An ordinary `lm` on the same rows, without the person, keeps the estimate at $0.42$ and inflates the standard error to $0.28$, so $p = 0.14$. A [random intercept]{.mark}, `(1 | ind)`, keeps $0.42$ and brings the standard error back to $0.14$. The $t$ statistic returns to $2.99$, the paired test.
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
![](figures/generated/sketch-nongauss-a-paired-lines.png){.sketch fig-alt="Five blue lines join each person's before and after values; they sit at different heights, marked between people in red, and fall by the same amount."}
:::
::::

In that fit the person-level variance is $3.06$ and the residual variance is $0.96$. Dropping the pair does not change the estimate. It charges the within-person contrast with the between-person noise.

::: {.notes}
Naive `lm` inflates SE to $0.28$, $p=0.14$; `(1|ind)` returns SE $0.14$ and $t=2.99$. Person variance $3.06$ versus residual $0.96$ on the slide. Dropping the pairing does not move the $0.42$ estimate—it adds between-person noise to the wrong error.

**Going further.** With person variance $\sigma_b^2$ and residual variance $\sigma^2$, the random-intercept model implies a compound-symmetric covariance for each person: $\operatorname{Var}(Y_{ij}) = \sigma_b^2 + \sigma^2$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{i1}, Y_{i2}) = \sigma_b^2$. The within-person difference has variance $2\sigma^2$, free of $\sigma_b^2$, so $\mathrm{SE} = \sqrt{2 \times 0.96 / 100} \approx 0.14$, against $\sqrt{2 \times (3.06 + 0.96)/100} \approx 0.28$ when the pairing is ignored. The intraclass correlation is $3.06/(3.06 + 0.96) \approx 0.76$. For complete, balanced pairs the REML fit reproduces the paired $t$ test exactly; Pinheiro and Bates, *Mixed-Effects Models in S and S-PLUS* (2000), derive it.
:::
## When ordinary least squares is the wrong skeleton {#sec-ols-replacements}

If the Gaussian, independent, constant-variance assumptions fail, the replacements are still models.

- Generalised least squares: a known pattern for the variance, which is the Welch test when the pattern is a group.
- Generalised estimating equations: a [working correlation]{.mark} and a sandwich standard error.
- A generalised linear model: a distribution for $Y$ and a link for $\mu$.
- A generalised additive model: a smooth function of $x$ in place of a straight line.

This hour then stays with the generalised linear model. The others are named so a later choice is a choice of estimand, not a new religion.

::: {.notes}
Four bullets: GLS, GEE, GLM, GAM—each names what breaks in OLS. This hour stays on GLM; the list prevents swapping religion when the estimand should change. Welch as GLS for group variance is the bridge back to earlier slides.

**Going further.** With $\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}) = \sigma^2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ known, Aitken's theorem makes $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathrm{GLS}} = (\mathbf{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{Y}$ the best linear unbiased estimator, by applying Gauss–Markov to $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\mathbf{Y}$. In practice $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ is estimated (feasible GLS, `nlme::gls`), which is efficient asymptotically but not exact in small samples. GEE instead keeps $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ simple and corrects only the standard error, trading efficiency for robustness to a wrong $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$.
:::
## `aov()` is Type I {#sec-anova-type}

![A warning that aov() in R is Type I ANOVA, so the test of treatment depends on whether baseline or treatment is entered first.](figures/sources/ancova-type-i-order.jpeg){fig-alt="Four rows. lm, car::Anova with type 2, and permuco are marked safe. aov is marked not safe, because the order of baseline and treatment changes the sums of squares." width="78%"}

[Olszewski](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7444337265641684992/): `aov()` is [Type I]{.mark}, so the treatment $F$ in his sketch is 16.6 or 38.7 depending on order. `car::Anova(type = 2)` does not inherit that order.

::: {.notes}
Treatment $F$ is 16.6 or 38.7 depending on entry order in Olszewski's sketch. `car::Anova(type=2)` is marked safe on the figure. Ask what happens if baseline and treatment are swapped in `aov()`.
:::
## Three types, then a deviance {#sec-deviance .smaller}

- **Type I:** each term after the terms written before it
- **Type II:** each main effect after the other main effects; an interaction after the mains
- **Type III:** each term after every other term, including interactions

The three answer different questions. Pick one before fitting, and do not use Type I unless the order is the scientific order.

For a generalised linear model the same partition is an [analysis of deviance]{.mark}. The statistic is a likelihood-ratio $\chi^2$, or a score test, rather than an $F$ on residual sums of squares. `anova(glm(...), test = "LRT")` is that comparison of nested models. It is still a test of a term in a model, not a new model. His 2025 notes put the conditional mean, the probability, the quantile, and the hazard on one page as the functions that comparison can target.

::: {.notes}
Type I, II, III definitions are different questions—pick before fitting. GLM partition is analysis of deviance with LRT, not $F$ on SS. His 2025 note bundles mean, probability, quantile, hazard as comparison targets—one line, do not over-read.

**Going further.** Type II respects marginality (Nelder, *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series A*, 1977): a main effect is not tested in the presence of an interaction that contains it. Type III does test it, and its sums of squares depend on the contrast coding, so it is meaningful only with sum-to-zero contrasts (`contr.sum`), not R's default treatment contrasts. For a GLM, the deviance difference between nested models is asymptotically $\chi^2$ with the difference in parameters (Wilks' theorem); when $\phi$ is estimated, as in a quasi-Poisson fit, the ratio to $\hat{\phi}$ is referred to an $F$ instead.
:::
## Favour the model, not a pretest

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 10
%%| fig-height: 2.8
flowchart LR
  question["Question"]
  support["Support of $$Y$$"]
  family["$$Y \mid x \sim \mathrm{family}(\mu)$$"]
  check["Residual plot"]
  report["Estimate and interval"]
  question --> support --> family --> check --> report
```

A [pretest]{.mark} that switches you from a $t$-test to a rank test still does not estimate $\mu = \mathbb{E}(Y \mid x)$. Rank tests answer a different contrast, and they have assumptions of their own.

The teaching sequence for the three models follows the SIB day on logistic regression and GLMs ([slides](https://github.com/sib-swiss/advanced-statistics/blob/master/docs/assets/pdf/Day2-LogisticregressionandGLM-2026.pdf), [course](https://www.sib.swiss/training/course/20260907_ADDMG)).

::: {.notes}
Walk the Mermaid: question → support → family → residual plot → estimate. Pretest switching $t$ to ranks still misses $\mu$. SIB day link is for students who want the full logistic/GLM course—optional aside.
:::
## Two names, one role each {#sec-lm-names}

[Angelino and Marcone](https://www.sib.swiss/training/course/20260907_ADDMG) (SIB, Lausanne, September 2026) use two roles. The **response**, also called the dependent variable, is what the model describes or predicts. That is $Y$ on the [notation](#sec-notation) slide.

The **explanatory variable** is also called an independent variable, a predictor, or a covariate. That is $x$. The question picks it. The general line is $Y = f(x) + \text{error}$. A function $g(Y)$ on the left is a transformed response, which is the case the [previous slides](#sec-log-estimand) treat as a change of estimand.

::: {.notes}
Response $Y$ versus explanatory $x$; $g(Y)$ on the left is the transformed-response case from earlier. Angelino and Marcone SIB attribution. Link notation slide if someone asks for $\mathbf{x}$.
:::
## The formula is the model {#sec-lm-formula}

In R the same line is `response ~ predictors`. Read `~` as "described by".

::: {.incremental}
- `+` adds a term. `-` or `-1` drops one, including the intercept.

- `:` is an interaction. `*` is the interaction and the main effects. `^n` adds interactions up to degree $n$.

- `I()` is arithmetic. `age^2` in a formula is not $age^2$. The square is `I(age^2)`.
:::


`y ~ 1` is the [null model]{.mark}: the mean, and no covariate. One mixed formula example is `Income ~ age^2 + I(weight/height^2) + gender`.

::: {.notes}
Step fragments: `+`/`-`, `:`/`*`/`^n`, `I()` for arithmetic. `y~1` is intercept-only. `age^2` in a formula is not squared age—`I(age^2)` is. Mixed example at the bottom is one sentence.
:::
## One row, then every row {#sec-lm-matrix}

For one observation,

$$
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_{p-1} x_{i,p-1} + \varepsilon_i.
$$

Stacked, that is $\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$. The first column of $\mathbf{X}$ is 1 when the model has an intercept. Least squares chooses $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ to minimise the sum of squared vertical residuals. The fitted values are $\hat{\mathbf{Y}} = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{Y}$, and $\mathbf{H}$ is the [hat matrix](#sec-hat).
