![](figures/generated/sketch-nongauss-a-matrix.png){.sketch-sm fig-alt="Block picture of Y equals X beta plus epsilon: a green column Y, a grey matrix X whose first column of ones is yellow, a red column beta, and a grey column epsilon, with one blue row i across Y and X." fig-align="center"}

::: {.notes}
Display $Y_i=\beta_0+\cdots+\varepsilon_i$, then $\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$. $\hat{\mathbf{Y}}=\mathbf{H}\mathbf{Y}$ introduces the hat matrix for leverage later.
:::
## Ordinary least squares is BLUE {#sec-gauss-markov}

The [Gauss–Markov theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%E2%80%93Markov_theorem): if $\mathbb{E}(\varepsilon_i) = 0$, the $\varepsilon_i$ are uncorrelated, each has the same finite variance $\sigma^2$, and $\mathbf{X}$ has full column rank, then

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{Y}
$$

has the smallest variance among [linear unbiased]{.mark} estimators. The errors do not have to be Gaussian for that result. Gauss used normality. Markov removed it.

If, in addition, the $\varepsilon_i$ are independent and Gaussian, that same $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ is the maximum-likelihood estimator. The $t$ tests and the $F$ test on the printout use this extra assumption. If the variances differ or the errors are correlated, the corresponding estimator is generalised least squares, which is the [Welch case](#sec-ols-replacements) when the variance is a group.

::: {.notes}
Gauss–Markov needs zero mean, uncorrelated equal-variance errors, full-rank $\mathbf{X}$—not Gaussian errors for BLUE. Gaussianity enters for MLE and for $t$/ $F$ on the printout. GLS is named when variance differs.

**Going further.** Gauss–Markov restricts the competition to linear unbiased estimators: a biased estimator such as ridge regression, or the James–Stein estimator when $p \ge 3$, can have a smaller mean squared error. Without Gaussian errors, $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ is still asymptotically normal, with covariance $\sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})^{-1}$, provided no single row of $\mathbf{X}$ dominates (the Lindeberg condition, $\max_i h_{ii} \to 0$); the $t$ and $F$ tests are then approximately valid for large $n$. With Gaussian errors the result strengthens to minimum variance among all unbiased estimators, since OLS attains the Cramér–Rao bound.
:::
## A coefficient is a $t$ {#sec-lm-t}

`summary(lm)` tests each coefficient against 0. The statistic is the estimate divided by its standard error. [Angelino and Marcone](https://www.sib.swiss/training/course/20260907_ADDMG) note that this test assumes Gaussian residuals. It is the interesting test for a slope. It is rarely the question for the intercept.

In a model with several covariates, each line is the test of that coefficient **with the other terms already in the model**. [Mahanty](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/interpreting-linear-model-output-r-anil-mahanty/) (9 January 2018) maps the same printout. Two of his readings do not travel: multiple $R$ is not a count of points on the line, and a small $p$ is not a verdict that the model fits.

::: {.notes}
Each `summary(lm)` line tests that coefficient with others already in. Mahanty's two warnings: multiple $R$ is not a point count; small $p$ is not goodness of fit. Intercept $t$ is rarely the scientific question.

**Going further.** Under independent Gaussian errors, $(\hat{\beta}_k - \beta_k)/\mathrm{SE}(\hat{\beta}_k)$ has an exact $t_{n - p}$ distribution because $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ and $\hat{\sigma}^2$ are independent and $(n - p)\hat{\sigma}^2/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{n - p}$ (Cochran's theorem). Without normality the ratio is asymptotically standard normal under the conditions of the previous slide. $\mathrm{SE}(\hat{\beta}_k) = \hat{\sigma}\sqrt{\{(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\}_{kk}}$ grows when $x_k$ is correlated with the other columns, by the variance inflation factor $1/(1 - R_k^2)$.
:::
## The $F$ test compares two nested models {#sec-lm-f}

The $F$ statistic on the same printout compares the fitted model with the [intercept-only model]{.mark}. The statistic is the drop in the residual sum of squares, per extra parameter, divided by the remaining residual mean square:

$$
\frac{\{\mathrm{SS}(\mathrm{mean}) - \mathrm{SS}(\mathrm{fit})\}/(p_{\mathrm{fit}} - p_{\mathrm{mean}})}{\mathrm{SS}(\mathrm{fit})/(n - p_{\mathrm{fit}})}.
$$

With a single slope, this $F$ matches the $t$ test of that slope. With several slopes, every coefficient can be quiet and the $F$ test can still reject. $R^2$ is the share of the variance of $Y$ that the fit captures. Adjusted $R^2$ charges a cost for each extra term. The residual degrees of freedom are $n$ minus the number of estimated parameters.

::: {.notes}
Read the $F$ ratio formula once; with one slope it matches slope $t$. Several quiet slopes can still yield a significant $F$. $R^2$ and adjusted $R^2$ definitions are on the slide—df is $n$ minus parameter count.

**Going further.** Under Gaussian errors and the null that the extra $q = p_{\mathrm{fit}} - p_{\mathrm{mean}}$ coefficients are zero, the ratio is exactly $F_{q,\, n - p_{\mathrm{fit}}}$. With $q = 1$ it equals the square of the $t$ statistic of that coefficient. It is a monotone function of the likelihood-ratio statistic for Gaussian models, so it is the small-sample version of the deviance test used for GLMs. $R^2$ never decreases when a term is added; adjusted $R^2 = 1 - (1 - R^2)(n - 1)/(n - p)$ can.
:::
## A factor shifts the intercept {#sec-lm-ancova}

The height example is `Height ~ Age + Gender`. Gender is a factor, so R codes it as an indicator against a reference level. Women are the baseline in the printout. The line for women is $124.52 + 2.72\,\mathrm{Age}$. The line for men has the same slope and a higher intercept, $127.3 + 2.72\,\mathrm{Age}$.

That is an [analysis of covariance]{.mark}: one continuous covariate, one categorical factor, and a common slope unless you add `Age:Gender`. The gender coefficient is a difference of intercepts, not the raw difference of the two mean heights. The sums of squares for that fit still depend on [which ANOVA type](#sec-anova-type) you ask for.

::: {.notes}
`Height~Age+Gender`: women $124.52+2.72\,\mathrm{Age}$, men same slope, higher intercept $127.3$. Gender coefficient is intercept difference, not raw mean difference. ANOVA type still matters for SS.
:::
## Four plots, then two more {#sec-lm-plot}

`plot()` on an `lm` draws four checks by default: residuals against fitted values, a normal QQ plot, scale against location, and residuals against leverage ([`plot.lm`](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/stats/versions/3.6.2/topics/plot.lm)). Those are `which = c(1, 2, 3, 5)`.

[Tay](https://www.r-bloggers.com/2019/11/the-hidden-diagnostic-plots-for-the-lm-object/) (14 November 2019) notes the two that are not in that panel. `which = 4` is [Cook's distance]{.mark} against the row number. `which = 6` is Cook's distance against leverage over one minus leverage. He treats a Cook's distance above 1 as a point to inspect. The next four slides are the default four, each with a fit that respects the assumption and a fit that does not. Illustrative draws, seed `20261005`.

::: {.notes}
Default `plot(lm)` is which 1,2,3,5; Tay adds Cook vs index (4) and Cook vs leverage (6). Cook $>1$ to inspect. Next four slides are the default panel, seed 20261005 illustrative fits.
:::
## Residuals against the fitted values

![Two residual-versus-fitted plots. Left: a flat cloud around zero. Right: a U-shape from fitting a straight line to a quadratic.](figures/generated/lm-resid-fitted.png){fig-alt="Left, residuals from a straight-line fit sit in a flat band around zero. Right, residuals from a straight line fitted to a quadratic curve form a U." width="96%"}

A flat cloud is the linear mean. A curve means $f(x)$ is still in the residual.

::: {.notes}
Left panel flat cloud is the linear mean assumption; right U-shape is missing curvature in $f(x)$. Pair with the smoothing section later. This is the first of four diagnostic figures—code was on the prior slide.
:::
## The residual QQ plot

![Two normal QQ plots of residuals. Left: points along the line. Right: heavy tails from a t distribution.](figures/generated/lm-qq.png){fig-alt="Left, Gaussian residuals follow the normal reference line. Right, residuals from a heavy-tailed draw flare at both ends." width="92%"}

Same reading as the [shape figures](#sec-qq-shapes). A line supports the Gaussian assumption behind the $t$ and $F$ tests. A flare is a heavy tail, and the next slide changes the model for $Y$.

::: {.notes}
Gaussian residuals on the line; $t$ residuals flare both tails. Same vocabulary as the opening QQ shapes. Flare here motivates changing the family for $Y$, not only the mean structure.
:::
## Scale against location {#sec-lm-scale-location}

![Two scale-location plots. Left: a flat smooth of the square-root absolute residual. Right: the smooth rises because the variance grows with x.](figures/generated/lm-scale-location.png){fig-alt="Left, the square root of the absolute residual stays level across fitted values. Right, it rises as the fitted value increases." width="96%"}

A flat smooth is [constant variance]{.mark}, the Gauss–Markov condition. A rise is a variance that travels with the mean: [generalised least squares](#sec-ols-replacements), or a family in which the variance depends on $\mu$.

::: {.notes}
Flat smooth of $\sqrt{|\text{residual}|}$ is constant variance; rising smooth is variance with mean. Link to $\phi V(\mu)$ in GLMs and to GLS on the replacements slide.
:::
## Leverage and Cook's distance

![Two residual-versus-leverage plots. Left: points near the origin, inside the Cook contours. Right: one point far to the right with a large residual.](figures/generated/lm-leverage.png){fig-alt="Left, residuals sit at small leverage. Right, one observation has high leverage and a large residual, beyond a Cook's-distance contour." width="96%"}

[Leverage]{.mark} $h_{ii}$ is the diagonal of the hat matrix. A common cut is $2p/n$ or $3p/n$ from Belsley, Kuh, and Welsch (1980). The contours are Cook's distance 0.5 and 1.

::: {.notes}
Leverage $h_{ii}$ from the hat matrix; cuts $2p/n$ or $3p/n$ from BKW. Cook contours 0.5 and 1 on the figure. High leverage plus large residual is the point to name on the right panel.

**Going further.** The leverage $h_{ii} = \mathbf{x}_i^{\top}(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{x}_i$ lies in $[0, 1]$ and the $h_{ii}$ sum to $p$, so their mean is $p/n$ and $2p/n$ flags twice the average. Cook's distance is $D_i = e_i^2 h_{ii} / \{p\, \hat{\sigma}^2 (1 - h_{ii})^2\}$, the scaled change in all fitted values when row $i$ is deleted; it combines a large residual with a large leverage. A cut of 1 corresponds roughly to moving $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ to the edge of a 50% confidence region (Cook and Weisberg, *Residuals and Influence in Regression*, 1982). For a GLM the same quantities come from the weighted hat matrix of the final IRLS step.
:::
## A model for the mean {.center .pitfall-divider background-gradient="linear-gradient(160deg, #f7f4ef 0%, #d5eadf 100%)"}

## The link acts on $\mu$, not on $Y$ {#sec-glm-link-mean}

Agresti writes a generalised linear model as one object: a distribution for $Y$, a [linear predictor]{.mark}, and a link on the conditional mean [@agrestiFoundationsLinearGeneralized2015].

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Link on the mean**

::: model
$$
g(\mu_i) = \mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}
$$
:::

After the fit, $\mathbb{E}(Y \mid \mathbf{x}) = g^{-1}(\mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta})$ is a probability, an expected count, or a positive rate.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Transform of $Y$**

$$
g(Y_i) = \mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \varepsilon_i
$$

That sentence rewrites each observation before the fit. It targets $\mathbb{E}\{g(Y)\}$, which is not $g(\mu)$ when $g$ is nonlinear.
:::
::::

The [estimand slides](#sec-log-estimand) are what the second column costs.

::: {.notes}
Left column: $g(\mu_i)=\mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}$. Right column transforms each $Y_i$ and targets $\mathbb{E}\{g(Y)\}$. Walk both callouts; estimand slides are the cost of the right column.

**Going further.** The families of a GLM are exponential dispersion models, $f(y; \theta, \phi) = \exp\{(y\theta - b(\theta))/a(\phi) + c(y, \phi)\}$, with $\mu = b'(\theta)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Y) = a(\phi)\, b''(\theta)$. The link $g$ connects $\mu$ to $\eta = \mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}$; the canonical link is the one with $\theta = \eta$. Nelder and Wedderburn (*Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series A*, 1972) introduced the class, and McCullagh and Nelder, *Generalized Linear Models* (1989), is the standard reference; Agresti [@agrestiFoundationsLinearGeneralized2015] gives the modern treatment.
:::

## The family matches the type of $Y$ {#sec-glm-family-match}

Ordinary least squares on a transformed response still carries a Gaussian error on whatever scale you chose.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
A GLM keeps $Y$ on its support and changes the [family]{.mark}:

- Bernoulli or binomial for a 0/1 outcome or a proportion
- Poisson for a non-negative integer count
- Gaussian on the identity link when that support is appropriate
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
![](figures/generated/sketch-nongauss-a-support.png){.sketch fig-alt="Three supports: two blue dots at 0 and 1 for Bernoulli, green dots at 0, 1, 2 and on along an arrow for Poisson, and a violet double arrow for Gaussian."}
:::
::::

The [family table](#sec-family-table) is the first menu. The point here is that the likelihood is written for $Y$, not for $g(Y)$.

::: {.notes}
OLS on $g(Y)$ still assumes Gaussian errors on the transformed scale. GLM list: Bernoulli/binomial, Poisson, Gaussian identity. Likelihood is written for $Y$, not $g(Y)$—family table is next.

**Going further.** The maximum-likelihood score equations of any GLM are $\sum_i \frac{(Y_i - \mu_i)}{\phi V(\mu_i)} \frac{\partial \mu_i}{\partial \boldsymbol{\beta}} = \mathbf{0}$. They depend on the family only through the mean model and the variance function. Wedderburn (*Biometrika*, 1974) used this to define quasi-likelihood: specify only $\mu(\mathbf{x})$ and $V(\mu)$, solve the same equations, and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ remains consistent and asymptotically normal if the mean is right. The full family matters for the likelihood itself, for prediction intervals, and for anything that uses the shape beyond two moments.
:::
## Variance travels with $\mu$ {#sec-glm-variance-mu}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Constant variance**

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y \mid \mathbf{x}) = \sigma^2
$$

This is the classical linear-model assumption. A fan on [scale against location](#sec-lm-scale-location) is the picture that it has failed.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Variance tied to the mean**

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i) = \phi\, V(\mu_i)
$$

Poisson: $V(\mu) = \mu$. Binomial mean $\pi$: variance $\pi(1-\pi)$. The link is part of the family, not a fix applied to the residuals afterwards.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Left: $\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid x)=\sigma^2$. Right: $\phi V(\mu)$ with Poisson $V(\mu)=\mu$ and binomial $\pi(1-\pi)$. Fan on scale-location is the picture for the left column failing.

**Going further.** In an exponential dispersion family the variance function $V(\mu) = b''\{(b')^{-1}(\mu)\}$ determines the family within the natural exponential families. Morris (*Annals of Statistics*, 1982) shows that exactly six have a quadratic $V$: Gaussian, Poisson, gamma, binomial, negative binomial, and the generalised hyperbolic secant. The Tweedie class, $V(\mu) = \mu^p$, interpolates: $p = 0$ Gaussian, $p = 1$ Poisson, $p = 2$ gamma, and $1 < p < 2$ a compound Poisson–gamma with exact zeros. The dispersion $\phi$ is 1 for Poisson and binomial; a Pearson estimate $\hat{\phi} = \sum_i (Y_i - \hat{\mu}_i)^2/V(\hat{\mu}_i)/(n - p)$ well above 1 is overdispersion.
:::
## The link keeps $\mu$ in range {#sec-glm-link-range}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
$\mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}$ can be any real number. The [inverse link]{.mark} maps it into the support of $\mu$.

- $\operatorname{logit}(\pi) = \mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}$ forces $0 < \pi < 1$
- $\log(\mu) = \mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}$ forces $\mu > 0$
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
![](figures/generated/sketch-nongauss-a-link-map.png){.sketch fig-alt="A long double arrow labelled x transpose beta, any real number, with blue arrows labelled g inverse funnelling every point into a short green segment from 0 to 1."}
:::
::::

A straight line on a transformed $Y$ does not give the same guarantee on the mean of the original response. That is why the [link stays on the mean](#sec-glm-versus-transform), not on $Y$.

::: {.notes}
Logit forces $0<\pi<1$; log link forces $\mu>0$. A line on $\log Y$ does not guarantee a valid mean on the original scale—inverse link does on $\mu$.

**Going further.** The fit is by iteratively reweighted least squares, which is Fisher scoring: regress the working response $z_i = \eta_i + (Y_i - \mu_i)\, g'(\mu_i)$ on $\mathbf{X}$ with weights $w_i = 1/\{V(\mu_i)\, g'(\mu_i)^2\}$, and repeat until $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ settles. With the canonical link (logit for binomial, log for Poisson, inverse for gamma), the observed and expected information coincide, so Fisher scoring equals Newton–Raphson and $\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{Y}$ is sufficient. The working response is a linearised $g(Y)$, which is why the link never needs $g(Y_i)$ to exist at $Y_i = 0$. Asymptotically $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \approx \mathcal{N}\{\boldsymbol{\beta}, \phi(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\}$.
:::
## Coefficients read on the link scale {#sec-glm-coef-meaning}

The link is chosen so $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ answers a substantive question on the mean.

For $\log(\mu) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$,

$$
\frac{\mu(x+1)}{\mu(x)} = e^{\beta_1}.
$$

For a logit on $\pi$, $e^{\beta_1}$ is an [odds ratio]{.mark}. The goal is not to make a histogram look Gaussian. The goal is a coefficient that names an effect on $\mu$. The compact contrast is [the link stays on the mean](#sec-glm-versus-transform).

::: {.notes}
For $\log\mu=\beta_0+\beta_1 x$, $\mu(x+1)/\mu(x)=e^{\beta_1}$. Logit: $e^{\beta_1}$ is an odds ratio. Goal is substantive effect on $\mu$, not a pretty histogram.

**Going further.** Wald intervals are computed on the link scale, $\hat{\beta}_1 \pm 1.96\, \mathrm{SE}$, and then exponentiated, which keeps a ratio positive; profile-likelihood intervals (`confint()` on a `glm`) are more accurate in small samples. The odds ratio approximates the risk ratio only when $\pi$ is small. The odds ratio is also non-collapsible: adding a covariate unrelated to treatment can change it, even in a randomised trial, because the marginal and conditional odds ratios differ (Greenland, Robins, and Pearl, *Statistical Science*, 1999). A log-linear rate ratio is collapsible in that sense.
:::
## The response chooses the family {#sec-family-table}

| Support of $Y$ | A first model |
| --- | --- |
| Continuous, unrestricted, stable variance | Gaussian linear model |
| Two categories, truly binary | Logit, $Y \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\pi)$ |
| Non-negative integer, variance near the mean | Poisson, log link |
| Same, with extra-Poisson variance | Negative binomial, log link |

The next slides keep $\mu = \mathbb{E}(Y \mid x)$ and change the family. A transformation of $Y$ is the other route, already set aside on the [estimand slides](#sec-log-estimand).

::: {.notes}
Table rows: continuous stable variance → Gaussian; binary → logit; count near equidispersion → Poisson; extra variance → negative binomial. Transformation route is explicitly set aside via log-estimand link.

**Going further.** Goodness of fit for a GLM is judged by the residual deviance $D = 2\{\ell(\text{saturated}) - \ell(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\}$, which is approximately $\chi^2_{n - p}$ only when every expected count is large; for sparse counts or binary $Y$ the reference distribution fails and residual plots are the better check. The negative binomial NB2 has $V(\mu) = \mu + \mu^2/\theta$, a gamma mixture of Poissons; it is not an exponential dispersion family unless $\theta$ is fixed, so `MASS::glm.nb` alternates between $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ and $\theta$. Hilbe, *Negative Binomial Regression* (2011), covers the variants.
:::
## The link stays on the mean {#sec-glm-versus-transform}

[Angelino and Marcone](https://www.sib.swiss/training/course/20260907_ADDMG) write the earlier models as $g(Y) = f(x) + \text{error}$. On a 0/1 response that line can return a probability below 0, because a straight line is not confined to $(0, 1)$.

In the generalised linear model the linearity sits on $g(\mu)$. The family then draws $Y$. The quantity you report is still a mean of the response you measured.

::: {.notes}
Angelino and Marcone: $g(Y)=f(x)+\text{error}$ on 0/1 can predict outside $(0,1)$. GLM linearises $g(\mu)$; family draws $Y$. Reported quantity remains mean of measured $Y$.

**Going further.** A linear probability model, least squares on a 0/1 $Y$, is unbiased for the slope of $\mathbb{E}(Y \mid x)$ when that mean really is linear, but $\operatorname{Var}(Y \mid x) = \pi(1 - \pi)$ is heteroskedastic by construction, so it needs a sandwich standard error, and its fitted values can leave $[0, 1]$. The logistic model is the canonical-link GLM for the Bernoulli family, so its score equations $\sum_i \mathbf{x}_i (Y_i - \hat{\pi}_i) = \mathbf{0}$ make the fitted and observed totals agree within every level of a factor in $\mathbf{x}$.
:::
## One skeleton for all three :link: {#sec-skeleton}

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 10
%%| fig-height: 2.4
flowchart LR
  fam["$$Y_i \mid x_i \sim \mathrm{family}(\mu_i)$$"]
  link["$$g(\mu_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i$$"]
  mean["$$\mu_i = g^{-1}(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i)$$"]
  fam --> link --> mean
```

- **Family:** how $\mathrm{Var}(Y \mid x)$ depends on $\mu$
- **Link** $g$: the scale on which $\beta_1 x$ is linear
- **Mean** $\mu = \mathbb{E}(Y \mid x)$: what $\beta$ describes, after you invert $g$

Agresti is the reference for the theory and the worked models [@agrestiFoundationsLinearGeneralized2015]. Estimation is by [maximum likelihood]{.mark}, not by a normal test of $Y$. The letters are fixed on the [notation](#sec-notation) slide.

::: {.notes}
Mermaid: family → link → $\mu=g^{-1}(\eta)$. Three bullets map to variance structure, scale of $\beta$, and mean after inversion. Agresti citation is the theory anchor; MLE not normal test on raw $Y$.

**Going further.** Each family here is a one-parameter exponential family, $f(y;\theta,\phi) = \exp\{[y\theta - b(\theta)]/a(\phi) + c(y,\phi)\}$, so $\mu = b'(\theta)$ and $\mathrm{Var}(Y) = a(\phi)\,b''(\theta) = \phi V(\mu)$: the variance function $V$ is what "family" means on this slide. The canonical link is $g = (b')^{-1}$, which gives the identity, the logit and the log for the Gaussian, Bernoulli and Poisson. With the canonical link, $\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{y}$ is sufficient for $\boldsymbol\beta$ and the score equations reduce to $\mathbf{X}^{\top}(\mathbf{y}-\boldsymbol\mu) = \mathbf{0}$. Nelder and Wedderburn's 1972 paper unified the three cases; McCullagh and Nelder's *Generalized Linear Models* is the classical derivation, and Agresti the modern one [@agrestiFoundationsLinearGeneralized2015].
:::
## A continuous response, on the identity {#sec-glm-gaussian}

A continuous response goes to a linear regression. The drawing is Gaussian, and the link is the [identity]{.mark}, so $\mu$ and the linear predictor are the same number.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 10
%%| fig-height: 2.2
flowchart LR
  x["$$x$$"] --> eta["$$\eta = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$$"]
  eta --> mu["$$\mu = \eta$$"]
  mu --> y["$$Y \mid x \sim \mathrm{Normal}(\mu,\sigma^2)$$"]
```

::: {.notes}
Identity link: $\mu=\eta$. Mermaid ends at Normal$(\mu,\sigma^2)$. This is linear regression dressed in GLM notation—bridge for students who only know `lm`.
:::

## What $\sigma$ does to a Gaussian {#sec-density-gaussian}

![Three normal densities. Widening sigma flattens the curve. Shifting the mean moves it.](figures/generated/density-gaussian.png){fig-alt="Three normal density curves. One has mean 0 and standard deviation 1. One has mean 0 and standard deviation 2 and is flatter. One has mean 1.5 and standard deviation 1." width="88%"}

These are the density functions, not a sample and not CA-SYS. $\sigma$ changes the spread. The mean shifts the curve. The two parameters are separate, which is the Gaussian case the [variance function](#sec-glm-variance-mu) gives up.

::: {.notes}
Point at the flat red curve first: same mean, larger $\sigma$. Then the blue shift. Illustrative densities from `scripts/generate-density-curves.R`. Twenty seconds.
:::

## A binary response, on the logit {#sec-glm-bernoulli}

A binary response goes to a [logistic regression]{.mark}. Here $\mu = \pi = \Pr(Y = 1 \mid x)$. The logit is the link used here. The probit is the alternative they mention later, and it stays close to this curve.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 10
%%| fig-height: 2.2
flowchart LR
  x["$$x$$"] --> eta["$$\mathrm{logit}(\pi) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$$"]
  eta --> pi["$$\pi = \mu$$"]
  pi --> y["$$Y \mid x \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\pi)$$"]
```

::: {.notes}
$\mu=\pi=\Pr(Y=1\mid x)$; logit link in the diagram. Probit mentioned as later alternative—stay on logit for odds-ratio reading.
:::
## A count, on the log {#sec-glm-poisson}

A count goes to a [Poisson regression]{.mark}. The mean is often written as $\lambda$. That symbol is $\mu$ on these slides. The log link keeps $\mu > 0$, and $\exp(\beta_1)$ is a multiplicative change in the mean count.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 10
%%| fig-height: 2.2
flowchart LR
  x["$$x$$"] --> eta["$$\log \mu = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$$"]
  eta --> mu["$$\mu = \exp(\eta)$$"]
  mu --> y["$$Y \mid x \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\mu)$$"]
```

Four working assumptions: $Y$ is a count per unit of time or space; $\log \mu$ is linear in $x$; the observations are independent; and $\mathrm{Var}(Y \mid x) = \mu$.

::: {.notes}
$\lambda$ on the slide is $\mu$ here; $\exp(\beta_1)$ multiplies mean count. Four assumptions at the bottom—especially $\mathrm{Var}(Y\mid x)=\mu$—are what CA-SYS will break.

**Going further.** Under the log link the Poisson log-likelihood is $\sum_i (y_i\eta_i - e^{\eta_i})$ up to a constant, so the score is $\mathbf{X}^{\top}(\mathbf{y}-\boldsymbol\mu)$ and, with an intercept, the fitted counts add up to the observed total; a factor covariate reproduces each group total exactly. The estimator of $\boldsymbol\beta$ stays consistent when the counts are not Poisson, provided $\log\mu$ is correctly specified: this is the pseudo-maximum-likelihood result of Gourieroux, Monfort and Trognon (1984, *Econometrica*). What breaks is the standard error, which relies on $\mathrm{Var}(Y\mid x)=\mu$; a sandwich estimator or a variance model repairs it (Cameron and Trivedi, *Regression Analysis of Count Data*).
:::
## The fit maximises the likelihood {#sec-glm-mle}

The fit is by maximum likelihood. For a Gaussian linear model that maximiser is the least-squares fit. For the logit and the Poisson log link there is no closed form: the estimates come from an [iterative algorithm]{.mark}.

The Newton step for the logit, from the chapter embedded [below](#sec-burakov), uses the Bernoulli variances as weights:

$$
\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t+1)} = \boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)} + (\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}^{(t)}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^{\top}(\mathbf{y} - \boldsymbol{\pi}^{(t)}),
\qquad w_i = \pi_i(1-\pi_i).
$$

::: {.notes}
The course notes state that the maximiser is iterative and do not write the update. The displayed step is Burakov's equation (2.87), in the chapter embedded later. $\mathbf{W}$ is diagonal. At convergence, $(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X})^{-1}$ is the estimated covariance of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$.

**Going further.** The general algorithm is iteratively reweighted least squares: regress the working response $z_i = \eta_i + (y_i-\mu_i)\,g'(\mu_i)$ on $\mathbf{X}$ with weights $w_i = 1/\{V(\mu_i)\,g'(\mu_i)^2\}$, and repeat. This is Fisher scoring; with the canonical link the observed and expected information coincide, so it is also Newton–Raphson, and for the logit $w_i = \pi_i(1-\pi_i)$ as on the slide. Under regularity conditions (fixed $p$, information growing with $n$, true value inside the parameter space), $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ is consistent and approximately $\mathrm{Normal}\{\boldsymbol\beta, \phi(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\}$. The maximiser need not exist: for a logit under separation the likelihood increases without bound, the failure on the checks figure. McCullagh and Nelder's *Generalized Linear Models* gives the derivation.
:::

## Hat values and Cook's distance, again {#sec-glm-influence}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
The same two diagnostics carry over. Keep the [hat-value]{.mark} cut at $2p/n$ or $3p/n$, the cut already used for the [linear model](#sec-lm-plot).

A [Cook's distance]{.mark} above about $4/n$ is the cut in the [SIB notes](https://www.sib.swiss/training/course/20260907_ADDMG), and a Cook's distance above 1 is [Tay's](https://www.r-bloggers.com/2019/11/the-hidden-diagnostic-plots-for-the-lm-object/) cut for `plot(lm)`, also printed on the [checks figure](#sec-glm-checks): two sources, so quote the one you use.
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
![](figures/generated/sketch-nongauss-b-leverage.png){.sketch fig-alt="Hand-drawn scatter: a cluster of black points at low x and one red point far to the right, labelled high h, pulls a solid red line upward away from the green dashed line fitted without it."}
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Hat cut $2p/n$ or $3p/n$ as for `lm`. Say aloud that $4/n$ is the SIB cut and 1 is Tay's cut for `plot(lm)`; they are not two versions of one rule. Next slide is residual types.

**Going further.** For a GLM the hat matrix is $\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{W}^{1/2}\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}^{1/2}$, taken from the last IRLS step (Pregibon, 1981, *Logistic regression diagnostics*, *Annals of Statistics*). Its trace is still $p$, which is why the $2p/n$ cut carries over, but $h_{ii}$ now depends on the fitted mean as well as on $\mathbf{x}_i$: in a logit, a point with an extreme $x$ and $\hat\pi_i$ near 0 or 1 gets a small weight and can have a small leverage. R's `cooks.distance()` for a `glm` uses the one-step approximation $D_i = r_{P,i}^2\,h_{ii}/\{\hat\phi\,p\,(1-h_{ii})^2\}$, with $r_{P,i}$ the Pearson residual, rather than refitting without observation $i$ (Williams, 1987, *Applied Statistics*).
:::
## Three residual scales {#sec-glm-resid}

Three residuals are worth plotting after a GLM.

::: {.incremental}
- A [deviance residual]{.mark}, plotted against the fitted value and against each covariate. A curve is a missing piece of the linear predictor.

- A [Pearson residual]{.mark}, $(Y - \mu)$ divided by the fitted standard deviation. A trend against a covariate is a term the model does not yet contain.

- A [quantile residual]{.mark}. Under the fitted family it is uniform on $(0,1)$. A QQ plot against normal quantiles is the picture. Extra-large tails are a signal to leave the Poisson for a quasi-Poisson or a negative binomial.
:::


`acf()` is a quick check that the observations are not ordered in a way the independence assumption forbids. The Poisson simulation later draws the quantile residual for that family.

::: {.notes}
Step deviance, Pearson, quantile residuals and what curve each catches. Quantile residuals uniform under the fitted family—QQ against normal is the plot. `acf()` flags ordered dependence.

**Going further.** With $d_i$ the contribution of observation $i$ to the deviance, the deviance residual is $\mathrm{sign}(y_i-\hat\mu_i)\sqrt{d_i}$ and the Pearson residual is $(y_i-\hat\mu_i)/\sqrt{\hat\phi\,V(\hat\mu_i)}$. Both are only approximately normal, and for binary data or small counts they fall in bands, one per observed value, so a residual-against-fitted plot shows stripes whatever the model. The quantile residual is Dunn and Smyth's (1996, *Randomized quantile residuals*, *Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics*): $r_i = \Phi^{-1}(u_i)$, with $u_i$ uniform between $F(y_i^-;\hat\mu_i)$ and $F(y_i;\hat\mu_i)$. If the model is correct and its parameters known, the $r_i$ are exactly independent standard normal; with estimated parameters this holds asymptotically. The `DHARMa` package builds the same residual by simulating from the fitted model, which also covers mixed models.
:::
## Two tiers of checks for a logit {.fit-fig #sec-glm-checks}

![Two tiers of logistic-regression checks: linearity of the log-odds, VIF, independence, Cook's distance; then separation, events per variable, and sparse categories.](figures/sources/logistic-model-checks.svg){fig-alt="Tier 1: a straight line on the log-odds scale, a VIF warning above 5 and a red flag above 10, independence as a design problem, and Cook's distance above 1. Tier 2: a zero cell and huge odds ratios, at least 10 events per variable as a rule of thumb that some recent work relaxes, and a category with no events to collapse." width="96%"}

🔗 [The checks figure](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7483052950236401665/). A bent log-odds line, a variance-inflation factor above 5, [separation]{.mark}, and fewer than ten events per variable are its warnings. Firth's penalised likelihood is the remedy it names for separation.

::: {.notes}
The LinkedIn post is behind a login wall, so the thresholds are the figure's own wording: VIF above 5 is a warning and above 10 a red flag; Cook's distance above 1 is a cause for concern; ten events per variable is a rule of thumb the figure says some recent work relaxes. Angelino and Marcone's Cook cut for a GLM is about $4/n$, stated on the previous influence slide.

**Going further.** Albert and Anderson (1984, *Biometrika*) showed that the logistic maximum-likelihood estimate exists and is finite only when the two outcome classes overlap: under complete or quasi-complete separation some $\hat\beta$ runs to $\pm\infty$, and R reports fitted probabilities of 0 or 1 with huge standard errors. Firth (1993, *Biometrika*) penalises the log-likelihood by $\tfrac12\log|\mathbf{I}(\boldsymbol\beta)|$, the Jeffreys prior, which removes the first-order bias and always gives finite estimates; Heinze and Schemper (2002, *Statistics in Medicine*) proposed it for separation, and `logistf` implements it with profile penalised-likelihood intervals. The ten-events-per-variable rule comes from simulation studies (Peduzzi and colleagues, 1996); van Smeden and colleagues (2016) argued that no single threshold guarantees good performance.
:::

## Deviance is the residual sum of squares {#sec-glm-deviance}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
Lack of fit is measured by the [deviance]{.mark}. The null deviance $D_0$ compares the intercept-only model with the [saturated model]{.mark}. The residual deviance $D$ compares the fitted model with the saturated model. Maximising the log-likelihood is the same operation as making $D$ small.
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
![](figures/generated/sketch-nongauss-b-deviance.png){.sketch fig-alt="Hand-drawn log-likelihood axis with three dots, null in grey, fitted in blue, saturated in green; a long arrow D0 spans null to saturated and a shorter blue arrow D spans fitted to saturated, under the formula D equals 2 times l-sat minus l."}
:::
::::

For nested models the [likelihood-ratio statistic]{.mark} is the drop in deviance,

$$
D_{\text{small}} - D_{\text{large}} \sim \chi^2,
$$

with degrees of freedom equal to the number of extra parameters. In R that is `anova(model1, model2, test = "Chisq")`. This is the GLM form of the [analysis of deviance](#sec-deviance).

::: {.notes}
Their pseudo-$R^2$ is $1 - D/D_0$. They say that several pseudo-$R^2$ exist, and that a nested comparison should be the likelihood-ratio test. AIC is the comparison they allow when the models are not nested: deviance, plus a penalty for the number of parameters.

**Going further.** The scaled deviance is $D/\phi = 2\{\ell_{\text{sat}} - \ell(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})\}$, and $\phi = 1$ for the Poisson and the Bernoulli. Wilks' theorem makes $(D_{\text{small}} - D_{\text{large}})/\phi$ approximately $\chi^2_q$ for nested models, with $p$ fixed and $n \to \infty$; when $\phi$ is estimated, as in the quasi-Poisson, the reference is an $F$ distribution (`test = "F"`). The residual deviance itself is $\chi^2_{n-p}$ only under small-dispersion asymptotics, large Poisson means or large binomial totals, because the saturated model gains a parameter with every observation. For 0/1 data the deviance is a function of the $\hat\pi_i$ alone and says nothing about fit; use a grouped check such as Hosmer–Lemeshow, or the residual plots. McCullagh and Nelder's *Generalized Linear Models* treats these limits.
:::

## Quantile residuals check the family

These are [randomised quantile residuals]{.mark} for a Poisson mean: if the family is right, they should look Gaussian. A heavy upper tail is a reason to leave the Poisson, not a reason to run Shapiro–Wilk on the raw counts.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
lower <- ifelse(y <= 0, 0, ppois(y - 1L, lambda = mu_hat))
upper <- ppois(y, lambda = mu_hat)
residual <- qnorm(runif(length(y), min = lower, max = upper))
```

::: {.notes}
Walk the code first: each count is spread uniformly over its step of the fitted distribution function, then mapped to the normal scale. The figure is on the next slide.
:::
## Quantile residuals check the family

![Two QQ plots of randomised Poisson quantile residuals. The Poisson sample tracks the reference line. The overdispersed sample lifts in the upper tail.](figures/generated/qq-quantile-residuals.png){fig-alt="QQ plots of randomised quantile residuals from a Poisson fit to Poisson counts and from a Poisson fit to overdispersed counts." width="96%"}

::: {.notes}
Walk the code, then the QQ plot. Stress that the reference is the fitted family, not marginal normality of the counts. Ask whether a heavy upper tail would change the variance model before they quote a rate ratio. About one minute.
:::

## What $\lambda$ does to a Poisson {#sec-density-poisson}

![Poisson probabilities for lambda 2, 8, and 20.](figures/generated/density-poisson.png){fig-alt="Three Poisson probability plots. Lambda 2 is piled near zero. Lambda 8 is wider. Lambda 20 is wider still and shifted right. The spread grows with the mean." width="88%"}

$\mathrm{Var}(Y) = \lambda = \mathbb{E}(Y)$. A larger mean is a wider plot. Illustrative probabilities from `scripts/generate-density-curves.R`, not a soil count.

::: {.notes}
The right-hand comb is both higher and wider. That is the one-parameter constraint. If their counts are wider than this picture, the next family is the negative binomial.
:::

## Poisson · when the count matches the story {auto-animate=true}

Use it when $Y$ is a non-negative integer and, to a first approximation, $\mathrm{Var}(Y \mid x) = \mu$.

::: {data-id="pois-eq"}
$$
\log \mu = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x.
$$
:::

Colony counts on a plate are the clean case. Sequence reads are a count too, but with two complications: the [sampling effort]{.mark} differs between samples, and the counts are more variable than a Poisson.

::: {.notes}
$\log\mu=\beta_0+\beta_1 x$ with data-id animate. Colony counts are clean; reads need offset and extra variance—foreshadow CA-SYS. Var equals mean is the assumption to test first.
:::

## Poisson · the CA-SYS version {auto-animate=true}

::: {data-id="pois-eq"}
$$
\log \mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \mathrm{tilled}_i + \mathrm{year}_i + \log(\text{library size}_i).
$$
:::

$Y$ is the number of *Nitrospira* reads in a sample: a nitrite-oxidising genus, 153,771 reads across the 595 samples. The last term is the [offset](#sec-casys-offset), so $\beta_1$ is a ratio of rates per read.

::: {.notes}
Point out that the equation changed in two places from the previous slide: year entered as a factor, and the offset appeared. Neither is cosmetic. Without the offset, a sample sequenced twice as deeply looks twice as rich in Nitrospira.
:::

## Poisson · the call {#sec-casys-poisson-code}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
casys <- read.csv("data/derived/casys_teaching.csv")

fit_pois <- glm(
  nitrospira_reads ~ tillage + factor(year) + offset(log(total_reads)),
  family = poisson, data = casys
)

# Is one parameter doing both jobs?
sum(residuals(fit_pois, "pearson")^2) / fit_pois$df.residual
#> 10.6
```

A Poisson sets $\mathrm{Var}(Y \mid x) = \mu$. A [Pearson statistic]{.mark} of 10.6 per degree of freedom says the data are about ten times more variable than that.

::: {.notes}
Run this if the laptop allows. The dispersion statistic is the number to look at before reading any coefficient, because the coefficient will look fine and the standard error will not. The rule of thumb is that a value near 1 is consistent with the Poisson; 10.6 is not a borderline case.

**Going further.** The statistic is the moment estimator of the dispersion, $\hat\phi = X^2/(n-p)$ with $X^2 = \sum_i (y_i-\hat\mu_i)^2/V(\hat\mu_i)$; under a correct Poisson model $X^2$ is approximately $\chi^2_{n-p}$, so $\hat\phi$ is near 1. The quasi-Poisson fit keeps the Poisson estimates and multiplies every standard error by $\sqrt{\hat\phi}$; here $\sqrt{10.6} \approx 3.3$, close to the threefold widening the negative binomial gives a few slides on. The deviance-based estimate $D/(n-p)$ is less reliable when many $\hat\mu_i$ are small, which is why McCullagh and Nelder prefer the Pearson form. A formal check is the score test of Dean and Lawless (1989, *Journal of the American Statistical Association*).
:::

## Negative binomial · same mean, one extra parameter {#sec-nb-theta}

Keep the log link. Add a [dispersion parameter]{.mark} $\theta > 0$:

::: model
$$
\mathrm{Var}(Y \mid x) = \mu + \frac{\mu^2}{\theta}.
$$
:::

This is the `MASS::glm.nb` parameterisation: large $\theta$ means "close to Poisson". Agresti writes the same quadratic variance with a different symbol for the extra term [@agrestiFoundationsLinearGeneralized2015]. On these reads $\hat\theta = 29.3$.

::: {.notes}
Two readings of theta. Algebraically it is the inverse of the extra variance per unit of mean squared. Mechanistically it is a gamma-distributed latent rate, integrated out, which is the derivation on the Poisson-gamma slide. Stress that theta is not a second scientific effect to interpret.

**Going further.** If $\lambda = \mu\nu$ with $\nu \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\theta, \theta)$, so that $\mathbb{E}(\nu)=1$ and $\mathrm{Var}(\nu) = 1/\theta$, integrating $\nu$ out of $\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)$ gives $\Pr(Y=y) = \frac{\Gamma(y+\theta)}{\Gamma(\theta)\,y!}\left(\frac{\theta}{\theta+\mu}\right)^{\theta}\left(\frac{\mu}{\theta+\mu}\right)^{y}$, Cameron and Trivedi's NB2, with the quadratic variance on the slide. NB1, $\mathrm{Var}(Y) = (1+\delta)\mu$, has the quasi-Poisson's shape and is a different model. `MASS::glm.nb` alternates IRLS for $\boldsymbol\beta$ at fixed $\theta$ with a maximum-likelihood step for $\theta$ (Venables and Ripley, *Modern Applied Statistics with S*). Testing the Poisson against it puts $1/\theta = 0$ on the boundary of the parameter space, so the likelihood-ratio statistic is a 50:50 mixture of $\chi^2_0$ and $\chi^2_1$ and the naive $p$-value should be halved (Self and Liang, 1987, *Journal of the American Statistical Association*).
:::

## Same mean, three values of $\theta$ {#sec-density-nb}

![Negative binomial probabilities at mean 8 for theta 1, 5, and 50, with the Poisson of the same mean.](figures/generated/density-negbin.png){fig-alt="Probability plots at mean 8. Theta 1 is the widest, with a long right tail. Theta 50 sits close to the Poisson of the same mean." width="88%"}

The mean stays 8. Small $\theta$ puts more mass in the tail, because $\mathrm{Var}(Y) = \mu + \mu^2/\theta$. Large $\theta$ collapses toward the Poisson. Illustrative, from `scripts/generate-density-curves.R`.

::: {.notes}
Cover the grey Poisson last. Ask which $\theta$ matches a Pearson dispersion near 1. The answer is the large one. The CA-SYS $\hat\theta$ of 29 is in that direction, not at 1.
:::

## One mean, two variance assumptions {#sec-casys-nb}

![Rate ratio for tilled against no-till, with a Poisson interval and a much wider negative binomial interval.](figures/generated/casys-poisson-vs-nb.png){fig-alt="Two horizontal intervals for the same rate ratio of about 0.97. The Poisson interval spans roughly 0.962 to 0.982; the negative binomial interval spans 0.941 to 1.002 and crosses one." width="94%"}

| Family | Rate ratio | 95% interval |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Poisson | 0.972 | 0.962 to 0.982 |
| Negative binomial | 0.971 | 0.941 to 1.002 |

::: {.notes}
This is the slide to slow down on. The point estimate barely moves, 0.972 against 0.971, because both models use the same mean equation. The interval is 3.1 times wider. Under the Poisson the contrast is "detected"; under the negative binomial it crosses one. Nothing about the biology changed between the two rows, only an assumption about the variance. Ask the room which interval they would put in a paper.

**Going further.** The near-identical point estimates are expected: when $\log\mu$ is correctly specified, the Poisson score equations give a consistent $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ whatever the true variance (Gourieroux, Monfort and Trognon, 1984), and the negative binomial only re-weights observations, by $\mu_i/(1+\mu_i/\theta)$ instead of $\mu_i$. The two fits therefore differ in efficiency and, mostly, in the covariance matrix. A third option keeps the Poisson estimate with a sandwich covariance, valid under any variance function but less stable in small samples (`sandwich` package). Ver Hoef and Boveng (2007, *Ecology*) compare quasi-Poisson and negative-binomial weighting and suggest plotting binned squared residuals against $\hat\mu$ to choose between a linear and a quadratic variance.
:::

## Read the mean, then $\theta$ {#sec-nb-read}

::: {.incremental}
- The rate ratio is a statement about $\mu$, on the log link, per read
- $\theta$ is not a second effect; it describes [leftover variation]{.mark}
- A QQ plot of quantile residuals is the check, not a test that "selects NB"
- With the wider interval, 1.00 is compatible with these data
:::


A 2.9% lower rate under tillage would matter agronomically. These 595 samples cannot separate it from no difference.

::: {.notes}
The last line is the honest summary, and it is the pitfalls lesson applied to a real fit: the estimate is the result, and the interval says how much the data constrain it. Resist the temptation to call this a null finding. It is an imprecise estimate of a small contrast, which is a different sentence.
:::

## The wrong family, on a QQ plot {#sec-casys-qq}

![Two QQ plots of residuals for the Nitrospira reads. The Gaussian linear model departs from the line at both ends; the negative binomial quantile residuals track it.](figures/generated/casys-qq-family.png){fig-alt="Left panel, standardised residuals from a Gaussian linear model on raw read counts, curving away from the reference line. Right panel, negative binomial quantile residuals close to the line." width="96%"}

::: {.notes}
Left is what you get if you put these counts into lm(). Right is the family the offset and the dispersion were chosen for. This is the same diagnostic as the earlier QQ slides, now on a real response rather than a draw, and it is the reason the family question comes before the test question.
:::

## Same count, three implementations

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Poisson

$$
\log \mu = \mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \log(\text{library size}), \qquad \mathrm{Var}(Y \mid x) = \mu.
$$

Tilled against no-till: rate ratio **0.972** (0.962 to 0.982). Pearson $\chi^2/\mathrm{df} = 10.6$, so that interval is too narrow.

### Negative binomial

$$
\mathrm{Var}(Y \mid x) = \mu + \mu^2/\theta, \qquad \hat\theta = 29.3.
$$

Same mean equation: rate ratio **0.971** (0.941 to 1.002). The interval is 3.1 times wider and crosses 1.

### $\log(Y+1)$, then Gaussian

$$
\mathbb{E}\{\log(Y+1) \mid x\} = \mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}.
$$

That coefficient is not a rate ratio for $\mu$, and the library size no longer enters as an offset. The two means are not the same function of $x$.

:::

Arrow keys step the tabs. All three are fits to the CA-SYS reads, from [generate-data-figures.R](scripts/generate-data-figures.R), using [casys_teaching.csv](data/derived/casys_teaching.csv).

::: {.notes}
Tab through Poisson, NB, $\log(Y+1)$ Gaussian—arrow keys on slide. Rate ratio 0.972 vs 0.971, Pearson 10.6, $\hat\theta=29.3$, log-plus-one loses offset interpretation. Script path `generate-data-figures.R` if asked.
:::
## A count that is not Poisson {#sec-casys-richness}

![Observed richness by cropping system, in four yearly panels.](figures/generated/casys-richness-system.png){fig-alt="Boxplots with jittered points of observed OTU richness for systems SD1, SD2, TS1 and TS2, in panels for 2018 to 2021." width="96%"}

Richness is an integer, so the reflex is a Poisson. Pearson $\chi^2/\mathrm{df} = 27.8$ says otherwise: richness is a count of OTUs out of 10,633, [bounded above]{.mark} and driven by sequencing effort.

::: {.notes}
A useful corrective. "Integer" does not imply "Poisson". Richness here is the number of distinct OTUs detected, so it is closer to a capture problem than to a rate: it is bounded by the reference table and it rises with library size. The honest teaching answer is that observed richness is a biased estimator of richness, and that the estimator belongs to the diversity literature rather than to a GLM slide. Note the 2018 panel is the pre-treatment baseline.
:::

## Detection depends on how hard you looked {#sec-casys-logit}

![Fitted logit curves for Methylobacter presence against standardised log library size, one curve per tillage class, with 0/1 observations jittered.](figures/generated/casys-logit-detection.png){fig-alt="Two rising logistic curves for probability of detecting Methylobacter against standardised log library size, with confidence ribbons and jittered binary observations." width="92%"}

*Methylobacter* is a methane oxidiser, present in 35% of samples. The odds of detecting it multiply by **1.74** per standard deviation of log library size.

::: {.notes}
This is the logit on a real response, and the result is uncomfortable in a useful way: the strongest predictor of presence is not a treatment, it is sequencing effort. The tillage odds ratio from the same fit is 1.34, with an interval of 0.95 to 1.91, so it is not separable from no effect here. Any presence-absence analysis of sequencing data has to carry library size, exactly as the count model carries the offset.
:::

## Equidispersion is one parameter doing two jobs {#sec-count-equi}

StatHarbor Analytics, *Count Data Models: From Poisson to Zero-Inflated Models*, starts from $Y \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\mu)$ with $\mathbb{E}(Y) = \mathrm{Var}(Y) = \mu$. One rate controls the centre and the spread. The log link makes a one-unit step in $x_j$ multiply $\mu$ by $e^{\beta_j}$, a [rate ratio]{.mark}.

The Poisson fit is the one they keep when the conditional mean is close to the conditional variance, the zeros are no more numerous than the Poisson predicts, and events are independent inside a fixed exposure. When $\mathrm{Var}(Y) > \mathbb{E}(Y)$, the same fit understates the standard errors. They name [unobserved heterogeneity]{.mark}, omitted covariates, and clustering as the usual sources.

::: {.notes}
Poisson: $\mathbb{E}(Y)=\mathrm{Var}(Y)=\mu$; $e^{\beta_j}$ is rate ratio on log link. StatHarbor list when Poisson is OK versus when SEs are too small. Heterogeneity, omitted covariates, clustering as sources on the slide.

**Going further.** Dean and Lawless (1989) derived the score test of $\mathrm{Var}(Y)=\mu$ against $\mathrm{Var}(Y)=\mu+\alpha\mu^2$; it needs only the Poisson fit, and its statistic is $\sum_i\{(y_i-\hat\mu_i)^2 - y_i\}/\sqrt{2\sum_i\hat\mu_i^2}$, approximately standard normal under the Poisson. Cameron and Trivedi (1990, *Journal of Econometrics*) recast it as an auxiliary regression of $\{(y_i-\hat\mu_i)^2-y_i\}/\hat\mu_i$ on $\hat\mu_i$, without intercept, and test the slope. Overdispersion is not always heterogeneity: a missing offset, clustering, an excess of zeros, or a misspecified mean all inflate $X^2$. Underdispersion, $\hat\phi < 1$, also occurs, for counts bounded above for instance, and the negative binomial cannot represent it.
:::
## A gamma latent rate is a negative binomial {#sec-count-nb}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
The same derivation gives the negative binomial as a [Poisson–gamma compound]{.mark}: the Poisson rate is itself a gamma draw, and that draw is integrated out. The extra variance is unobserved heterogeneity.
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
![](figures/generated/sketch-nongauss-b-gamma-poisson.png){.sketch fig-alt="Hand-drawn violet gamma curve for lambda with three coloured draws; each draw feeds a narrow Poisson bump at its own place, and together they make one wide black bump labelled NB."}
:::
::::

$$
\mathrm{Var}(Y \mid x) = \mu + \frac{\mu^2}{\alpha}
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\mathrm{Var}(Y \mid x) = \mu + \alpha\mu^2.
$$

McCullagh and Nelder use the first form. The simulation slides call that shape $\theta$. In the second form, $\alpha \to 0$ returns the Poisson. Estimating $\alpha$ leaves the one-parameter exponential family.

::: {.notes}
Treating $\alpha$ as known keeps the model inside a one-parameter GLM. Estimating it is full maximum likelihood. StatHarbor reaches for the negative binomial when the variance exceeds the mean and the zeros come from the same process as the positive counts, and compares it with the Poisson by a likelihood-ratio test.

**Going further.** The derivation is two lines: $\mathbb{E}(Y) = \mathbb{E}(\lambda) = \mu$ and $\mathrm{Var}(Y) = \mathbb{E}(\lambda) + \mathrm{Var}(\lambda) = \mu + \mu^2/\theta$ when $\lambda$ is gamma with shape $\theta$ and mean $\mu$. Another mixing law gives another margin with a similar variance: a log-normal $\lambda$ also has $\mathrm{Var}(\lambda) \propto \mu^2$, so the Poisson log-normal shares the quadratic variance and differs in the tails. Greenwood and Yule (1920, *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society*) introduced this gamma mixture for accident counts; Hilbe's *Negative Binomial Regression* is the applied reference. The likelihood-ratio test against the Poisson has the boundary problem noted on the $\theta$ slide.
:::

## A point mass of zeros is a mixture {#sec-count-zip}

A zero-inflated model is a different generative story. With probability $\pi_0$ the observation is a [structural zero]{.mark}. With probability $1-\pi_0$ it is a draw from a count distribution $f$. StatHarbor writes $\pi_0$ as $p$.

$$
\Pr(Y=0) = \pi_0 + (1-\pi_0)\,f(0),
\qquad
\Pr(Y=k>0) = (1-\pi_0)\,f(k).
$$

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 10
%%| fig-height: 2.6
flowchart LR
  z["$$\pi_0$$"] --> zero["structural zero"]
  z --> count["$$1-\pi_0$$"]
  count --> f["$$f$$: Poisson or NB"]
  f --> y["$$Y$$"]
  zero --> y
```

A logit for $\pi_0$ plus a log-linear Poisson is the zero-inflated Poisson. The negative binomial in $f$ is the zero-inflated negative binomial. Neither is an exponential-family GLM.

::: {.notes}
StatHarbor compares a zero-inflated model with an ordinary Poisson by AIC, BIC, or a Vuong test, because those two models are not nested.

**Going further.** The zero-inflated Poisson is Lambert's (1992, *Technometrics*); it is fitted by maximum likelihood, or by EM with the latent structural-zero indicator. Vuong's test (1989, *Econometrica*) compares non-nested models through the mean and variance of the per-observation log-likelihood ratios. But the Poisson is the zero-inflated Poisson at $\pi_0 = 0$, on the boundary, so the two are in fact nested there and the Vuong reference distribution does not hold; Wilson (2015, *Economics Letters*) documents this misuse. A boundary-corrected likelihood-ratio test, or a plot of predicted against observed zero frequencies, is the safer check. A hurdle model (Mullahy, 1986, *Journal of Econometrics*) tells the other story: every zero comes from one binary process and the positives from a zero-truncated count.
:::

## Four count models, three questions {#sec-count-table}

| Model | Extra variance | Structural zeros | Exponential family |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Poisson | No | No | Yes |
| Negative binomial | Yes | No | Only if the dispersion is fixed |
| Zero-inflated Poisson | No | Yes | No |
| Zero-inflated negative binomial | Yes | Yes | No |

The practical line under the table: diagnose dispersion and extra zeros before you quote a rate ratio. An ill-matched family understates the uncertainty.

::: {.notes}
Table: extra variance, structural zeros, exponential family column. Practical line under table—diagnose before quoting a rate ratio. ZIP and ZINB are not GLMs in the strict sense.
:::
## The count measures a latent share {#sec-measure}

[Sarkar and Stephens](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41588-021-00873-4) separate a [measurement model]{.mark} from a model for the latent intensity. The paper is about genes in single cells. The same split applies to any feature counted inside a sample of finite depth: a taxon, a transcript, a fragment.

Let $s_i$ be the [library size]{.mark}, the total count in sample $i$, and let $\lambda_{i\ell}$ be the relative intensity of feature $\ell$, a share of that sample. The measurement model is

$$
Y_{i\ell} \mid s_i, \lambda_{i\ell} \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(s_i \lambda_{i\ell}).
$$

Dividing by the depth is this rate: the offset $\log s_i$, with its coefficient fixed at 1.

::: {.notes}
$Y_{i\ell}\mid s_i,\lambda_{i\ell}\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(s_i\lambda_{i\ell})$; offset $\log s_i$ with coefficient 1. Sarkar–Stephens single-cell paper, same logic for any feature in finite depth.

**Going further.** An offset is a covariate whose coefficient is fixed at 1: $\log\mu_i = \log s_i + \mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol\beta$ is $\mu_i/s_i = \exp(\mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol\beta)$, so $\boldsymbol\beta$ acts on the rate per read. Entering $\log s_i$ as an ordinary covariate and testing its slope against 1 checks that proportionality. Modelling $y_i/s_i$ with a Gaussian model is not equivalent: it discards the fact that the variance of a proportion falls with depth. Differential-abundance software often replaces the raw library size by a robust size factor, such as the median-of-ratios of Anders and Huber (2010, *Genome Biology*), because a few dominant features can distort the total.
:::
## The measurement drawing {#sec-measure-dag}

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 10
%%| fig-height: 2.4
flowchart LR
  lam["$$\lambda_{i\ell}$$"] --> rate["$$\mu_{i\ell}=s_i\lambda_{i\ell}$$"]
  s["$$s_i$$"] --> rate
  rate --> y["$$Y_{i\ell}\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\mu_{i\ell})$$"]
```

Library size and relative intensity meet in the Poisson mean. The Pearson-residual figure below is this regression, with the slope of $\log s_i$ fixed.

::: {.notes}
Mermaid: $\lambda$ and $s$ meet in $\mu=s\lambda$, then Poisson draw. Pearson-residual figure below is this regression with fixed log-depth slope.
:::
## Three assumptions in the measurement layer {#sec-box1}

Box 1 of Sarkar and Stephens lists the assumptions behind that Poisson measurement model.

::: {.incremental}
- In each sample, each molecule is equally likely to be observed.

- Each molecule is observed independently of the others.

- Only a small proportion of the molecules present are observed. They cite 10–20% in a typical single-cell experiment.
:::


Assumptions 2 and 3 are the ones they treat as plausible. Assumption 1 fails when stability, cellular location, or sequence changes the chance that a molecule is seen. A bias that is shared across samples can enter the Poisson model as a covariate. A bias that changes from sample to sample is extra noise, and the measurement model that carries it is negative binomial. If a later protocol observes a larger share of the molecules, the measurement variance falls relative to a Poisson.

::: {.notes}
Step fragments: equal capture probability (often fails), independence (plausible), small observed fraction 10–20% (plausible). Sample-specific bias → NB measurement model per slide text.
:::
## A zero is an observation {#sec-zeros}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="70%"}
Sarkar and Stephens refuse the phrase "missing data" for a zero count. The picture: a minute with no cars at an intersection is a zero; an hour when the observer is away is a [missing record]{.mark}. A sequencing zero is the first of those. Imputing only the zeros treats them as holes.
:::
::: {.column width="30%"}
![](figures/generated/sketch-nongauss-b-zeros.png){.sketch-sm fig-alt="Two hand-drawn empty crossroads: on the left a green observer with a note reading 0, labelled zero; on the right an empty red stool with a note reading a question mark, labelled missing."}
:::
::::

They also drop the word "dropout" for a supposed device that writes a zero whatever the true intensity. Spike-in controls, in the papers they cite, did not support a zero-inflated *measurement* model. A zero-inflated *observation* model can still be the right margin when the latent intensity itself has a point mass at zero.

::: {.notes}
Cars-at-intersection versus absent observer—sequencing zero is the first. No impute-only-zeros; spike-in evidence against dropout measurement model. ZI on latent intensity can still be right.
:::
## The observation model is the margin {#sec-obs-model}

An [expression model]{.mark} is a distribution $g_\ell$ for the latent share $\lambda_{i\ell}$. The [observation model]{.mark} is the distribution of $Y$ after $\lambda$ has been integrated out.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 10
%%| fig-height: 2.4
flowchart LR
  g["$$\lambda_{i\ell}\sim g_\ell$$"] --> poi["$$Y_{i\ell}\mid s_i,\lambda_{i\ell}\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(s_i\lambda_{i\ell})$$"]
  poi --> marg["margin of $$Y_{i\ell}$$"]
```

A gamma $g_\ell$ produces a negative-binomial margin. A point-gamma $g_\ell$, a spike at zero plus a gamma, produces a zero-inflated negative-binomial margin. The Poisson recommendation is for the measurement layer. The margin is usually wider, because the latent share varies across samples.

::: {.notes}
$g_\ell$ for latent $\lambda$; integrate to margin of $Y$. Gamma → NB margin; point-gamma → ZINB. Poisson recommendation is measurement layer; margin usually wider.
:::

| Point-gamma | Zero-inflated NB | PSCL |

| Fully nonparametric | Flexible | ashr |

Table 1 of Sarkar and Stephens. Each row is a latent model for one feature, combined with the Poisson measurement model. The method column is the software they list for that margin.

Table 1 Sarkar–Stephens: latent model row drives margin and software column. Point mass → Poisson analytic; gamma → edgeR/DESeq2 class tools. One row per feature with Poisson measurement.

| Link $h$ | Noise on the latent scale | Methods they name |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Identity | None | NMF, scHPF |
| Identity | Gamma | NBMF |
| Log | None | GLM-PCA |
| Log | Gamma | scNBMF, GLM-PCA |

| Neural network | Point-gamma | scVI, DCA |

Table 2. A multi-feature model writes the share through a [low-rank factorisation]{.mark} and a link $h$, then adds a noise distribution for the stochastic piece. Overdispersion relative to the Poisson measurement changes the variance of $Y$ and leaves the mean of the structured part to be read with that measurement model in mind.

Table 2: link $h$, noise on latent scale, named methods. ZINB-WaVE and scVI are multivariate—not the single-feature GLM from earlier. Overdispersion changes $Y$ variance, mean read with measurement model.
